p.seg: Classic of Southern Mountains, Section One
The beginning of the Southern Mountains is called Què Shān.
Its first mountain is called Zhāoyáo Shān,
overlooking the Western Sea.
It has much cinnamon,
and much gold and jade.
There is a plant there,
which looks like chives but has blue flowers.
Its name is Zhùyú,
and eating it prevents hunger.
There is a tree there,
which looks like a paper mulberry but has black veins.
Its flowers illuminate in all four directions.
Its name is Mígǔ,
and wearing it prevents getting lost.
There is an animal there,
which looks like a macaque but has white ears.
It crouches and walks like a human.
Its name is Xīngxīng,
and eating it makes one good at running.
The Lízhū River originates here
and flows westward into the sea.
There is much yùpèi within,
and wearing it prevents internal diseases.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east
is Tángtíng Shān,
which has many *yǎnmù* trees,
Many white apes;
many *shuǐyù* (water jade);
much gold.
Three hundred and eighty *lǐ* further east,
is called Jíyì Mountain.
Within it are many strange beasts;
the waters are full of strange fish;
many white jade;
many vipers;
many strange snakes;
many strange trees;
one cannot ascend it.
Three hundred and seventy *lǐ* further east,
is called Niǔyáng Mountain.
On its sunny side, there is much red gold;
on its shady side, much white gold.
There is a beast there,
its shape is like a horse but with a white head,
its markings are like a tiger but with a red tail,
its sound is like singing,
its name is Lùshǔ.
Wearing it ensures many descendants.
A strange river emerges from it,
and flows east into the Xiànyì River.
Within it are many dark turtles,
their shape is like a turtle but with a bird's head and a snake's tail,
Its name is Xuán Guī (旋龜),
its sound is like splitting wood.
Wearing it prevents deafness,
and it can be used as a base.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east is Zhī Shān (祗山),
with abundant water
and no grass or trees.
There is a fish there,
its appearance is like a cow,
it lives on hills,
it has a snake's tail and wings,
its wings are under its ribs,
its sound is like a bellowing cow,
its name is Lù (鯥),
it dies in winter and is born in summer.
Eating it prevents swelling diseases.
Four hundred *lǐ* further east
is Dǎn Yuán zhī Shān (亶爰之山),
with abundant water,
no grass or trees,
and is impossible to ascend.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a wildcat but with long hair,
its name is Lèi (類),
it reproduces by itself, without needing a partner of the opposite gender.
Eating it prevents jealousy.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east
It is called Jīshān 曰基山.
On its southern slope, there is much jade;
on its northern slope, there are many strange trees.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a sheep,
with nine tails and four ears,
its eyes are on its back.
Its name is Bóyí 猼訑.
Wearing it [a piece of its hide] makes one unafraid.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a chicken, but with three heads and six eyes,
six feet and three wings.
Its name is Shàngfù 上符.
Eating it prevents one from sleeping.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east,
is a mountain called Qīngqiū zhī Shān 青丘之山.
On its southern slope, there is much jade;
on its northern slope, there is much blue cyanotrichite.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a fox but with nine tails.
Its sound is like that of an infant,
and it can eat people.
Eating it prevents one from being afflicted by *gǔ* poisoning.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a dove,
its sound is like scolding.
Its name is Guànguàn 灌灌.
Wearing it prevents one from being deluded.
The Yīng River originates here and
flows south, emptying into the Jíyì Marsh.
Within it are many chìrú fish,
which resemble fish but have human faces.
Their sound is like that of mandarin ducks, and
eating them prevents scabies.
Three hundred and fifty *lǐ* further east is
Mount Jīwěi.
Its tail extends into the East Sea.
There are many sand and stones.
The Fāng River originates here and
flows south, emptying into the Yù River.
Within it are many white jade.
Altogether, the first of the Què Mountains,
from Mount Zhāoyáo
to Mount Jīwěi,
comprise ten mountains,
spanning two thousand nine hundred and fifty *lǐ*.
The appearances of their gods are all those of bird bodies and dragon heads.
The rituals for their sacrifices:
A single zhāng jade is buried with the animal offering,
the offerings consist of glutinous rice
and a single bì jade,
rice and
white *suān* grass are used as mats.
The beginning of the second Classic of the South
is called Mount Jǔ.
To the west it borders Liúhuáng,
to the north it faces Zhū Pí,
to the east it faces Chángyòu.
The Yīng River originates here,
flowing southwest to empty into the Chì River,
within which there is much white jade,
and much red millet.
There is a beast,
its shape is like a pig,
and it has spurs,
its sound is like a dog barking,
its name is Lílì,
its appearance indicates that the county will have much earthwork.
There is a bird,
its shape is like an owl but it has human hands,
its sound is like paralysis,
its name is Zhū,
its cry is a self-calling,
its appearance indicates that the county will have many exiled scholars.
Four hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the southeast
is called Mount Chángyòu,
where there is no grass or trees,
and much water.
There is a beast,
its shape is like an ape with four ears,
its name is Chángyòu,
its sound is like chanting,
its appearance indicates that the prefecture and county will have great floods.
Another three hundred and forty *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Yáoguāng (堯光之山).
Its southern slope has abundant jade,
and its northern slope has abundant metal.
There is an animal
that looks like a person but has the bristles of a pig.
It dwells in caves and hibernates in winter.
Its name is Huáihuái (猾褢),
and its sound is like chopping wood.
If it appears, there will be great forced labor in the district.
Another three hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the east
is called Mount Yǔ (羽山).
Below it, there is much water;
above it, there is much rain.
There are no grasses or trees,
but there are many vipers.
Another three hundred and seventy *lǐ* to the east
is called Mount Qúfù (瞿父之山).
There are no grasses or trees,
but there is abundant metal and jade.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the east
is called Mount Gōuyú (句餘之山).
There are no grasses or trees,
but there is abundant metal and jade.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east
is called Mount Fúyù (浮玉之山).
To the north, one can see Jùqū (具區);
to the east, one can see Zhūpí (諸毗).
There is an animal
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a tiger but with the tail of an ox,
its sound is like a barking dog,
its name is zhì 彘,
it eats people.
The Tiáo River originates from its northern side,
and flows north into the Jùqū 具區 lake.
There are many tī 鮆 fish in it.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is called Chéngshān 成山,
square-shaped with three terraces,
its top has much gold and jade,
its bottom has much qīngfū 青䨼.
The Yí River originates from it,
and flows south into the Hūsháo 虖勺 (lake),
there is much gold in it.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is called the mountain of Kuàijī 會稽之山,
square-shaped,
its top has much gold and jade,
its bottom has much fūshí 砆石 (inferior jade).
The Sháo River originates from it,
and flows south into the Jū 湨 (river).
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is called Yíshān 夷山,
without grass or trees,
much sand and stone,
the Jū River originates from it,
and flows south into the Liè Tú.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east is
Mount Pú Gōu,
whose summit is rich in gold and jade,
and whose base is rich in grasses and trees.
There are no birds or beasts
and no water.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east is
Mount Xián Yīn,
with no grasses or trees
and no water.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the east is
Mount Xún,
whose southern slope is rich in gold
and whose northern slope is rich in jade.
There is a beast there
which looks like a sheep but has no mouth.
It cannot be killed.
Its name is Huán.
The Xún River originates here
and flows south into the È Marsh,
which is abundant in *zǐluǒ* (purple snails).
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the east is
Mount Hū Sháo,
whose summit is rich in catalpa and *nán* trees,
and whose base is rich in thorny bushes and *qǐ* trees.
The Pāng River originates here
and flows eastward into the sea.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
there is a mountain called Qū Wú zhī Shān 區吳之山,
with no grass or trees,
and much sand and rock.
The Lù Shuǐ 鹿水 originates here,
and flows southward into the Pāng Shuǐ 滂水.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
there is a mountain called Lù Wú zhī Shān 鹿吳之山,
with no grass or trees on top,
and much metal and stone.
The Zé Gēng zhī Shuǐ 澤更之水 originates here,
and flows southward into the Pāng Shuǐ 滂水.
There is a beast here,
named Gǔ Diāo 蠱雕,
its appearance is like a hawk but with horns,
its sound is like the cry of an infant,
and it eats people.
Five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
there is a mountain called Qī Wú zhī Shān 漆吳之山,
with no grass or trees,
much *bó* stone,
and no jade.
It is situated by the sea,
looking eastward towards Qiū Shān 丘山,
whose light sometimes emerges and sometimes disappears,
Such is the order of the days.
In general, the beginning of the *Second Classic of the Southern Regions*
stretches from Guì Shān 柜山 to Qī Wú zhī Shān 漆吳之山,
encompassing seventeen mountains,
spanning seven thousand two hundred *lǐ*.
The shapes of their deities are all dragon bodies with bird heads.
For their sacrifices:
a single jade disk (*bì*) is buried for the offering of hair,
and glutinous rice (*tú*) is used as offering grains (*xǔ*).
The beginning of the *Third Classic of the Southern Regions*
is called Tiān Yú zhī Shān 天虞之山,
which has much water at its base,
making it impossible to ascend.
Five hundred *lǐ* to the east
is Dǎo Guò zhī Shān 禱過之山,
which has much gold and jade on its summit,
and many rhinoceroses (*xī*),
wild oxen (*sì*), and many elephants at its base.
There is a bird,
which is shaped like a *jiāo*
but has a white head, three feet, and a human face,
and is named Qú Rú 瞿如,
and its cry is its own name.
The Yín Shuǐ 泿水 River originates here
and flows south into the sea.
In it dwells the tiger *jiāo*,
whose shape is that of a fish's body with a snake's tail,
Its head is like that of a mandarin duck;
those who eat it will not develop swelling,
and it can cure hemorrhoids.
Five hundred *lǐ* further east is
Dān Xué zhī Shān 丹穴之山 (Mount Cinnabar Cave),
where there is much gold and jade.
The Dān Shuǐ 丹水 (Cinnabar River) originates here
and flows south into the Bohai Sea.
There is a bird here,
its shape is like a chicken,
with five-colored markings,
named Fènghuáng 鳳皇 (Phoenix).
The pattern on its head says "Virtue" (德, Dé),
the pattern on its wings says "Obedience" (順, Shùn),
the pattern on its back says "Righteousness" (義, Yì),
the pattern on its chest says "Benevolence" (仁, Rén),
the pattern on its belly says "Trustworthiness" (信, Xìn).
This bird
eats and drinks naturally,
singing and dancing by itself.
Its appearance signifies peace and tranquility throughout the world.
Five hundred *lǐ* further east is
Fā Shuǎng zhī Shān 發爽之山 (Mount Revealing Brilliance),
with no grass or trees,
but much water
and many white apes.
The Fàn Shuǐ 汎水 (Vast River) originates here
and flows south into the Bohai Sea.
Again, four hundred *lǐ* to the east,
one arrives at the tail of Mount Máo (Máoshān).
To its south is a valley
called Yùyí.
Many strange birds are found there.
The gentle south wind originates from this place.
Again, four hundred *lǐ* to the east,
one arrives at the head of Mount Fēi.
Gold and jade are abundant on its summit,
but there is no water.
Below, many vipers are found.
Again, five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is the mountain called Yángjiā.
There is no grass or trees,
but there is much water.
Again, five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is the mountain called Guànxiāng.
The summit is covered in trees,
but there is no grass;
many strange birds are found there,
but no beasts.
Again, five hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is the mountain called Jī (Jīshān).
Gold is abundant on its summit,
Below it, there is much red pigment and ochre.
The Hēi Shuǐ (Black River) originates here,
and flows southwards into the sea.
Within it there is the zhuān yú (鱄魚) fish,
its appearance is like a crucian carp but with pig bristles,
its sound is like a piglet,
its appearance portends a great drought in the world.
Further east four hundred *lǐ*,
is called the Língqiū zhī Shān (令丘之山) Mountain,
with no grass or trees,
and much fire.
To its south there is a valley,
called Zhōng Gǔ (中谷),
from which the tiáo fēng (條風) wind comes forth.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like an owl,
with a human face, four eyes and ears,
its name is yóng (顒),
its cry is its own name,
its appearance portends a great drought in the world.
Further east three hundred and seventy *lǐ*,
is called the Lúnzhě zhī Shān (侖者之山) Mountain,
above it there is much gold and jade,
below it there is much blue malachite.
There is a tree,
its appearance is like a paper mulberry tree but with red veins,
Its sweat is like lacquer,
its taste is like candy.
Those who eat it will not be hungry,
and it can relieve fatigue.
Its name is called bái yú,
and it can test jade.
Further east for five hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
there is a mountain called Yúgǎo zhī Shān,
which has many strange beasts
and many large snakes.
Eastward for five hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
there is a mountain called Nányú zhī Shān,
whose summit has abundant gold and jade,
and whose base has abundant water.
There is a cave there,
into which water always enters in the spring,
then emerges in the summer,
and closes in the winter.
The Zuǒ River originates there
and flows southeast to empty into the sea.
There are *fenghuang* and *yuanchu*.
In total, the head of the "Southern Classic, Third Section",
from Tiānyú zhī Shān to Nányú zhī Shān,
comprises fourteen mountains in all,
spanning six thousand five hundred and thirty *lǐ*.
Their deities all have dragon bodies and human faces.
Their sacrifices
all involve praying with a white dog,
and the offerings consist of fine rice.
This concludes the Southern Classic of mountains,
encompassing forty mountains in total, large and small,
spanning sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty *lǐ*.
Second Classic of the Western Mountains
"Classic of the Western Mountains": The first of the mountains of Huà Shān,
is called Mount Qiánlái.
On it are many pine trees,
and below it is much washstone.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a sheep but with a horse's tail,
its name is *xiányáng*,
its fat can cure chapped skin.
Forty-five *lǐ* further west
is called Mount Sōngguǒ.
The Guàn River originates there,
flowing north into the Wèi River,
and there is much copper within it.
There is a bird,
its name is *hóngqú*,
its appearance is like a pheasant,
with a black body and red feet,
and it can cure carbuncles.
Sixty *lǐ* further west
It is said that Mount Tài Huà,
is cut sharply and is four-sided.
Its height is five thousand *rèn*,
its width is ten *lǐ*,
and birds and beasts do not dwell there.
There is a snake there,
named Féi Yí,
with six feet and four wings;
when it appears, there will be a great drought in the world.
Eighty *lǐ* further west,
is Mount Xiǎo Huá.
Its trees are mostly thorny jujubes, its beasts are mostly *máo niú*,
its shady side has many chime stones,
its sunny side has many *xiū fú* jade.
There are many red *bì* birds,
which can ward off fire.
There is a grass there called *bì lì*,
which looks like crow-leek,
and grows on stones,
and also grows by climbing on trees.
Eating it can cure heart pain.
Eighty *lǐ* further west,
is Mount Fú Yú.
Its sunny side has much copper,
its shady side has much iron.
There is a tree on it,
named Wén Jīng,
Its fruit is like a jujube,
and can cure deafness.
Its grasses are mostly *tiáo*,
their appearance is like a sunflower,
with red flowers and yellow fruit,
like an infant’s tongue,
eating it makes people not bewildered.
The Fú Yú River originates here,
and flows north into the Wèi River.
Its animals are mostly cōng lóng,
their appearance is like a sheep but with a red mane.
Its birds are mostly mín,
their appearance is like a kingfisher but with a red beak,
and can ward off fire.
Sixty *lǐ* further west is
called Shí Cuī Mountain.
Its trees are mostly zōng nán,
its grasses are mostly *tiáo*,
their appearance is like chives,
with white flowers and black fruit,
eating them cures scabies.
On its south side, there is much bǎo fú jade,
on its north side, there is much copper.
The Guàn River originates here,
and flows north into the Yú River.
Within it there is flowing ocher,
using it to paint oxen and horses will keep them free from illness.
Seventy *lǐ* further west is
It is called Yīngshān.
On it, there are many *niǔjiāng* trees.
On its shady side, there is much iron.
On its sunny side, there is much red gold.
The Yú River originates here,
flowing north and emptying into the Zhāo River.
In it, there are many *zhìyú* fish,
which look like turtles
and sound like sheep.
On its sunny side, there are many *jiànshī* plants.
Among the animals, there are many yaks and *xiányáng* sheep.
There is a bird there,
which looks like a quail,
with a yellow body and a red beak.
Its name is Féiyí;
eating it will cure leprosy,
and it can kill insects.
Fifty-two *lǐ* further west,
is called Zhúshān.
On it, there are many tall trees.
On its shady side, there is much iron.
There is a plant there,
its name is Huánghuān;
it looks like an ailanthus tree,
and its leaves are like hemp.
It has white flowers and red fruit,
which look like ochre.
Bathing in it can cure scabies,
and can also cure skin diseases.
The Zhú Shuǐ (竹水) River originates here,
flowing north into the Wèi (渭) River.
On its south-facing side, there are many bamboo arrows
and much azure jade.
The Dān Shuǐ (丹水) River originates here,
flowing southeast into the Luò Shuǐ (洛水) River,
where there are many water jade and
many "human-fish."
There is an animal
that looks like a pig with white hair,
the hair as thick as a hairpin with black tips,
using its hair to shoot objects;
it is called háo zhì (毫彘).
Another 120 *lǐ* to the west is called Fú Shān (浮山),
where there are many pàn mù (盼木) trees,
with leaves like *zhǐ* (枳) orange trees but without thorns,
woodworms live in them.
There is a plant
called xūn cǎo (薰草),
with leaves like hemp but square stems,
red flowers and black fruit,
smelling like mí wú (蘼蕪);
wearing it can cure leprosy.
Another 70 *lǐ* to the west
Called Yú Cì zhī Shān,
the Qī River originates from it,
flowing north and emptying into the Wèi River.
On its upper slopes grow many yù jiāng trees,
below it are many bamboo arrows,
on its shady side is much red copper,
on its sunny side is much Yīng Yuán jade.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a monkey (yóu) but with long arms,
it is good at throwing,
its name is Xiāo.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like an owl (xiāo),
with a human face and one foot,
its name is Tuó Tuó,
it appears in winter and hibernates in summer,
wearing it makes one unafraid of thunder.
Further west by one hundred and fifty *lǐ*,
is called Shí Shān,
with no grass or trees.
The Zhú River originates from it,
flowing north and emptying into the Wèi River,
within it is much crystal.
Further west by one hundred and seventy *lǐ*,
is called Nán Shān,
above it grows much red millet.
The Dān River originates from it,
The Běiliú River flows into the Wèi River.
The beasts are mostly fierce leopards,
and the birds are mostly cūjiū (尸鳩).
Another 180 *lǐ* to the west is
called Dàshí Mountain.
The top is abundant with *gǔzuò* (榖柞),
the bottom is abundant with *niǔjiāng* (杻橿),
the shady side is abundant with silver,
and the sunny side is abundant with white jade.
The Cén River originates here,
flowing north into the Wèi River.
The Qīngshuǐ River originates here,
flowing south into the Hàn River.
Another 320 *lǐ* to the west is
called Bōzhǒng Mountain.
The Hàn River originates here,
and flows southeast into the Miǎn River.
The Xiāo River originates here,
flowing north into the Tāng River.
Its top is abundant with peach branch hooks,
the beasts are mostly rhinoceroses, *sì*, bears, and *pí*,
and the birds are mostly white hán (翰) and red bì (鷩).
There is a plant,
its leaves are like *huì*,
its roots are like *jiégěng* (桔梗),
it has black flowers but no fruit,
named *gūrong* (蓇蓉),
Eating it will cause a person to be childless.
Another 350 *lǐ* to the west is
Mount Tiāndì (天帝之山).
Its upper part is abundant with palm trees and *nán* trees,
and its lower part is abundant with *jiān* and *huì* plants.
There is an animal there,
its shape is like a dog,
its name is Xībiān (谿邊);
one who sits on its skin will not be afflicted by *gǔ* poisoning.
There is a bird there,
its shape is like a quail,
with black patterns and a red nape,
its name is Lì (櫟);
eating it will cure hemorrhoids.
There is a plant there,
its shape is like a sunflower,
its scent is like *míwú*,
its name is Dùhéng (杜衡);
it can cause horses to run faster,
and eating it will cure goiters.
380 *lǐ* to the southwest is
Mount Gāotú (皋塗之山).
The Tú River originates here
and flows west into the Zhūzī River,
the Tú River also originates here
and flows south into the Jíhuò River.
Its south-facing side is abundant with red millet,
On its shady side are many silver and gold deposits.
On its upper part are many cinnamon trees.
There is a white stone there,
its name is yǔ
which can be used to poison rats.
There is a plant there,
its appearance is like gǎo bá,
its leaves are like sunflowers but red on the back,
its name is Wútiáo,
which can be used to poison rats.
There is an animal there,
its appearance is like a deer but with a white tail,
horse's feet and human hands, and four horns,
its name is Juérú.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like an owl but with human feet,
its name is Shùsī,
eating it can cure goiter.
Further west for one hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
is called Huáng Shān,
which has no grass or trees,
but many bamboo arrows.
The Pàn River originates there,
flowing west and emptying into the Chì River,
in which there is much jade.
There is an animal there,
its appearance is like an ox,
but dark green and black with large eyes,
Its name is Yáo.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like an owl,
with blue feathers and a red beak,
having a human tongue and able to speak,
its name is Yīngwǔ.
Two hundred *lǐ* further west,
is called Cuìshān,
on top of it are many palm and *nán* trees,
below it are many bamboo arrows,
on its sunny side are much gold and jade,
on its shady side are many yaks, *líng* antelope, and musk deer.
Its birds are mostly *fú*,
their appearance is like magpies,
red and black with two heads and four feet,
they can ward off fire.
Two hundred and fifty *lǐ* further west,
is called Guīshān,
it is where the *dùn yú* (bell-like musical instrument) is cast into the Western Sea,
without grass or trees,
and abundant in jade.
The Qī River originates from it,
flowing westward into the sea,
within it are much colored stone and gold,
and abundant cinnabar.
In total, the beginning of the "Western Classic",
From Qiánlái zhī Shān (錢來之山) to Guī Shān (騩山),
in all nineteen mountains,
spanning two thousand nine hundred and fifty-seven *lǐ*.
Huà Shān (華山) is its principal mountain;
the ritual for its sacrifice:
a complete offering.
Yú Shān (羭山) is its deity;
the sacrifice to it uses candles,
with a hundred days of fasting and a hundred sacrificial animals,
and a soup burial with a hundred pieces of jade,
with a hundred barrels of wine,
adorned with a hundred *guī* and a hundred *bì*.
The remaining seventeen subordinate mountains,
are all sacrificed to with a complete animal offering of a single sheep.
The candles are made from un-ashed hundred grasses,
with white mats and pure colored silks.
The beginning of the "Second Classic of the West"
is called Qián Shān (鈐山).
There is much copper on it,
and much jade beneath it,
and its trees are mostly *niǔ jiāng*.
Two hundred *lǐ* to the west,
is called Tàimào zhī Shān (泰冒之山).
There is much gold on its sunny side,
and much iron on its shady side.
The Luò River (洛水) originates here,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Among them are many *zǎo yù* (藻玉, algae jade),
and many white snakes.
Another 170 *lǐ* to the west is
called Shùlì Zhī Shān (數歷之山, Mount Shuli),
on which there is much gold,
and beneath it is much silver.
Its trees are mostly *niǔ jiāng* (杻橿, species of trees),
and its birds are mostly parrots (*yīng wǔ*, 鸚䳇).
The Chǔ River (楚水) originates here
and flows south, emptying into the Wèi River (渭水),
where there are many pearls.
Another 150 *lǐ* to the west is called Gāo Shān (高山, High Mountain),
on which there is much silver,
and beneath it is much *qīng bì* (青碧, a blue-green mineral) and realgar (雄黃, *xióng huáng*).
Its trees are mostly palm trees (*zōng*, 椶),
and its grasses are mostly bamboo.
The Jīng River (涇水) originates here
and flows east, emptying into the Wèi River (渭水),
where there are many musical stones (*qìng shí*, 磬石) and *qīng bì* (青碧, a blue-green mineral).
300 *lǐ* to the southwest is
called Nǚchuáng Zhī Shān (女床之山, Mount Nüchuang),
on its sunny (south-facing) side there is much red copper,
and on its shady (north-facing) side there is much *shí niè* (石涅, black pigment).
Its beasts are mostly tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and *sì sì* (兕兕, a type of rhinoceros).
There is a bird,
which looks like a pheasant (*dí*, 翟) but has five-colored markings.
It is called the *luán niǎo* bird;
its appearance indicates that the world will be peaceful and tranquil.
Another two hundred *lǐ* to the west
is called Mount Lóngshǒu.
On its southern slope there is abundant gold,
and on its northern slope there is abundant iron.
The Tiáo River originates here,
flowing southeast to empty into the Jīng River,
and within it are many beautiful jades.
Another two hundred *lǐ* to the west
is called Mount Lùtái.
On its summit there is abundant white jade,
and at its base there is abundant silver.
The animals there are mostly *mó* oxen, *xián* goats, and white *háo*.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a male chicken but with a human face;
it is called *fú xī*.
Its cry is its own name.
Its appearance indicates that there will be warfare.
Two hundred *lǐ* southwest
is called Mount Niǎowēi.
On its southern slope there is abundant chimes-stone,
and on its northern slope there is abundant sandalwood and *chǔ* trees;
within it there are many *nǚ chuáng* plants.
The Niǎowēi River originates here,
flowing west to empty into the Chì River,
Among them are many crimson millet.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the west is
called Xiǎo Cì zhī Shān 小次之山.
On it are many white jades,
and below it are many red copper.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like an ape,
but with a white head and red feet,
its name is Zhū Yàn 朱厭.
Its appearance portends great warfare.
Another three hundred *lǐ* to the west is
called Dà Cì zhī Shān 大次之山.
On its south side is much white clay,
on its north side is much green jade,
its beasts are mostly *máo* cattle and antelope.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the west is
called Xūn Wú zhī Shān 薰吳之山.
There are no grasses or trees,
but much gold and jade.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the west is
called Dǐ Yáng zhī Shān 厎陽之山.
Its trees are mostly millet, *nán*, and *yùzhāng*,
its beasts are mostly rhinoceros, *sì*, tigers, *zhuó*, and *máo* cattle.
Another two hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the west is
It is called the Mountain of Many Beasts.
On its summit, there is an abundance of *qiúfú* jade.
At its base, there are many sandalwood and *chǔ* trees.
There is much gold.
The animals there are mostly rhinoceros and *sì*.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the west is
called the Mountain of the Huáng People.
On its summit, there is an abundance of gold and jade.
At its base, there is an abundance of green realgar.
The Huáng River originates here,
flowing westward into the Chì River.
Within it, there is an abundance of red millet.
Another three hundred *lǐ* to the west is
called the Central Huáng Mountain.
On its summit, there is an abundance of gold.
At its base, there is an abundance of fragrant orchid and *táng* trees.
Another three hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the west is
called the Western Huáng Mountain.
On its sunny side, there is much gold.
On its shady side, there is much iron.
The animals there are mostly elk and *líniú*.
Another three hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the west is
called Lái Mountain.
Its trees are mostly sandalwood and *chǔ* trees.
Its birds are mostly *luóluó*,
These eat people.
In general, the beginning of the Second Classic of the Western Range
extends from Qián Shān 鈐山 to Lái Shān 萊山,
encompassing seventeen mountains,
spanning four thousand one hundred and forty *lǐ* 里.
The ten spirits among them
all have human faces and horse bodies.
The seven spirits all have human faces and ox bodies,
with four feet and one arm,
wielding a staff to walk;
these are the spirits of flying beasts.
To sacrifice to them,
use a *shào láo* 少牢 (small offering) of hair,
and use white *jiān* 菅 grass for a mat.
As for the ten other types of spirits,
to sacrifice to them,
use a single male chicken for hair,
*qián* 鈐 (to seal or to mark) but without *xǔ* 糈 (offering of grain);
use colored hair.
At the beginning of the Third Classic of the Western Range,
there is a mountain called Chóng Wú zhī Shān 崇吾之山,
located south of the Hé 河 (Yellow River),
with Zhǒng Suì 冢遂 visible to the north,
and Yáo zhī Zé 䍃之澤 (Marsh of Yao) visible to the south,
Dì zhī Bó 帝之搏 (the Emperor’s Hunting Enclosure) and Shòu zhī Qiū 獸之丘 (Hill of Beasts) visible to the west,
and Tuó Yuān 䗡淵 (Tuo Abyss) visible to the east.
There is a tree there
It has round leaves and a white calyx;
red flowers and black veins;
its fruit is like a trifoliate orange;
eating it is good for descendants.
There is a beast,
it looks like a Yú 禺 but has patterned arms;
it resembles a leopard and a tiger and is good at throwing;
its name is Jǔfù 舉父.
There is a bird,
it looks like a wild duck,
but has one wing and one eye;
only together can they fly;
its name is Mǎnmǎn 蠻蠻,
its appearance forebodes great floods under heaven.
Three hundred *lǐ* northwest,
is called Mount Chángshā 長沙.
The Cǐshui 泚水 River originates here,
flowing north into the Yǒushuǐ 泑水 River;
there are no grasses or trees,
but an abundance of green realgar.
Again, three hundred and seventy *lǐ* northwest,
is called Mount Bùzhōu 不周.
To the north, one can see Mount Zhūpí 諸毗,
overlooking Mount Yuèchóng 嶽崇,
to the east, one can see the Yòuzé 泑澤 Marsh,
where the Hé 河 River lies hidden,
Its source is turbid and bubbling.
There grow fine fruits,
their fruits like peaches,
their leaves like jujubes,
with yellow flowers and red calyxes,
eating them requires no labor.
Further northwest four hundred and twenty *lǐ*,
is called Mount Mì.
On it are many cinnabar trees,
round leaves and red stems,
yellow flowers and red fruits,
their taste is like malt sugar,
eating them prevents hunger.
The Dān River originates there,
flowing west into the Jì Marsh,
in it are many white jade stones,
there is jade essence,
its source bubbling and gushing,
the Yellow Emperor, Huángdì, eats and enjoys it.
It produces dark jade.
The jade essence that comes out,
is used to nourish the cinnabar trees.
The cinnabar trees after five years,
their five colors become clear,
their five flavors become fragrant.
Huángdì then takes the jade bloom of Mount Mì,
and casts it on the south side of Mount Zhōng.
*Jǐn* and *yú* jade are considered good,
It is firm, dense, and precise,
turbid, black, and yet has a luster.
The five colors are exhibited,
harmonizing softness and strength.
Heaven, Earth, spirits, and deities,
use it for food and offerings;
the noble person wears it,
to ward off misfortune.
From Míshān 峚山 to Zhōngshān 鍾山,
it is four hundred and sixty *lǐ*, in between
is entirely marshland.
Here are many strange birds, bizarre beasts, and wondrous fish,
all extraordinary creatures.
Further northwest for four hundred and twenty *lǐ*,
is called Zhōngshān 鍾山.
Its offspring is named Gǔ 鼓,
it has the appearance of a human face and a dragon's body.
He and Qīnbīng 欽䲹 killed Bǎojiāng 葆江 on the sunny side of Kūnlún 崑崙.
The Di 帝 then executed them on the east side of Zhōngshān 鍾山, called Yáo'àn 瑤岸.
Qīnbīng 欽䲹 transformed into a great osprey,
its appearance like an eagle but with black markings,
white head, red beak, and tiger claws.
Its call is like a morning swan;
when it appears, there will be great war.
Gǔ 鼓 also transformed into a jùnniǎo 鵔鳥,
its appearance like an owl,
with red feet and a straight beak,
With yellow markings and a white head,
its sound is like that of a swan.
When it appears, there will be a great drought in its region.
Another one hundred and eighty *lǐ* to the west is
Mount Tàiqì.
The Guān River originates here,
flowing westward and emptying into the quicksand.
This place abounds with the wényáo fish,
which resembles a carp,
but has the body of a fish and the wings of a bird.
It has blue markings and a white head,
and a red beak.
It constantly travels the Western Sea,
and roams in the Eastern Sea,
flying at night.
Its sound is like that of a *luán* chicken.
Its taste is sour and sweet.
Eating it will cure madness.
When it appears, there will be a great harvest in the world.
Another three hundred and twenty *lǐ* to the west is
Mount Huáijiāng.
The Qiūshí River originates here,
flowing northward and emptying into the Yōu River.
It contains many luómǔ (snail mothers/pearl oysters).
On its summit, there is much green realgar.
Much *lánggān* (coral/precious stones) and jade, and gold are stored there.
On its southern side, there are many red foxtail millets.
On its shady side are many deposits of gold and silver.
In truth, it is the level garden of the Di (Emperor),
overseen by the spirit Yīng Zhāo;
its form is that of a horse's body with a human face,
tiger stripes, and bird wings;
it patrols the four seas,
its sound is like that of a pomegranate.
Looking south, one sees the Kūnlún Mountains,
its light blazing,
its aura swirling.
Looking west, one sees the Great Marsh,
where Hòujì hid;
within it is much jade,
and on its shady side are many fragrant yáo trees resembling ruò trees.
Looking north, one sees Zhū Pí,
where Huái Guǐ and Lí Lún dwell,
the dwelling place of eagles and hawks.
Looking east, one sees the four-terraced Mount Huán,
where the Qióng Guǐ dwell,
each in its own dwelling.
There is a long, flowing watercourse,
its clarity glistening.
There is a celestial spirit there,
its form like a cow,
but with eight feet, two heads, and a horse's tail,
its sound like *bóhuáng*;
its appearance portends warfare in the city.
Four hundred *lǐ* to the southwest,
is called the Hill of Kūnlún,
truly the Lower Capital of the Emperor,
the god Lù Wú oversees it.
This god has the form of a tiger's body with nine tails,
a human face and tiger claws;
this god
oversees the nine divisions of the heavens and the Emperor's gardens in their seasons.
There is a beast,
its form is like a sheep but with
four horns,
its name is Tǔlóu,
it eats people.
There is a bird,
its form is like a bee,
as large as a mandarin duck,
its name is Qīnyuán,
if it stings birds and beasts, they die,
if it stings trees, they wither.
There is a bird, its name is Chúnniǎo,
it oversees the Emperor's hundred garments.
There is a tree,
its form is like a *táng* tree,
with yellow and red blossoms and fruit,
its taste is like a plum but without a pit,
its name is Shātáng,
it can ward off water,
eating it prevents one from drowning.
There is a plant,
called the bīn cǎo (薲草),
which looks like the sunflower, and tastes like scallion.
Eating it alleviates fatigue.
The Hé Shuǐ (河水) River originates here,
and flows south, then east into the Wúdá (無達) River.
The Chì Shuǐ (赤水) River originates here,
and flows southeast into the Fàn Tiān (氾天) River.
The Yáng Shuǐ (洋水) River originates here,
and flows southwest into the Chǒu Tú (醜塗) River.
The Hēi Shuǐ (黑水) River originates here,
and flows west into the Dà Yú (大杅) River.
There are many strange birds and beasts.
Another 370 *lǐ* to the west is
called Mount Lèyóu (樂游).
The Táo Shuǐ (桃水) River originates here,
and flows west into the Jì Zé (稷澤) marsh.
There is much white jade here.
There are many téng yú (𩹂魚) within,
which look like snakes but have four feet;
they eat fish.
Traveling 400 *lǐ* west from here,
is called the Liú Shā (流沙), or Quicksand.
After 200 *lǐ* you arrive at Mount Luó Mǔ (蠃母).
The deity Cháng Chéng (長乘) oversees it;
it is one of the nine virtues of Heaven.
The deity looks like a person with the tail of a bào (犳).
On it is much jade;
beneath it is much bluish-gray stone, but no water.
Three hundred and fifty *lǐ* further west,
is called Yùshān (Jade Mountain),
the place where Xī Wángmǔ (the Queen Mother of the West) dwells.
The Xī Wángmǔ's appearance is like that of a human,
with a leopard's tail and tiger's teeth, and she is good at whistling.
She has disheveled hair and wears a *shèng* headdress.
She is in charge of the disasters of the heavens and the five destructive forces.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a dog but with leopard markings,
its horns are like those of a cow,
its name is Jiǎo,
its sound is like a barking dog,
when it appears, the country will have a great harvest.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a pheasant but red,
its name is Shèngyù,
it eats fish,
its sound is like *lù*,
when it appears, the country will have a great flood.
Four hundred and eighty *lǐ* further west,
is called Xuānyuán zhī Qiū (Mound of Xuānyuán),
where there is no vegetation.
The Xún River originates here,
flowing south and emptying into the Black River.
Among them are many cinnabar grains,
and much azure orpiment.
Three hundred *lǐ* further west,
is called Mount Jīshí (積石之山),
below it is a stone gate,
where the Yellow River emerges and flows southwest.
On this mountain,
all kinds of things are found.
Two hundred *lǐ* further west,
is called Mount Chángliú (長留之山),
where the deity Bái Dì Shào Hào (白帝少昊), the White Emperor Shào Hào, resides.
All its beasts have patterned tails,
and all its birds have patterned heads.
Here are many patterned jade and stones.
It is actually the palace of the round deity Kuǐshì (磈氏).
This deity
is in charge of reflected light.
Two hundred and eighty *lǐ* further west,
is called Mount Zhāng'é (章莪之山),
with no grass or trees,
but many fine jades.
What it produces is very strange.
There is a beast there,
which looks like a red leopard,
with five tails and one horn,
its sound is like striking a stone,
Its name is Zhēng (猙).
There is a bird,
its appearance is like a crane,
with one foot,
red markings, bluish-green body, and a white beak.
Its name is Bìfāng (畢方),
its cry is its own name.
When it appears, that town will have strange fires.
Three hundred *lǐ* further west,
is called Yīnshān (陰山).
The Zhuóyù (濁浴) River originates here,
and flows south into the Fānzé (蕃澤),
where there are many patterned shells.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a fox but with a white head,
its name is Tiāngǒu (天狗),
its sound is like "liú liú" (榴榴),
it can ward off misfortune.
Two hundred *lǐ* further west,
is called Mount Fúdàng (符愓).
The top of it has many palm and *nán* trees,
the bottom of it has much gold and jade.
The deity Jiāng Yí (江疑) dwells there.
This mountain
often has strange rains
and is where wind and clouds originate.
Two hundred and twenty *lǐ* further west,
is called Mount Sānwēi (三危).
Three Bluebirds dwell there.
This mountain extends a hundred *lǐ* in all directions.
On it there is a beast,
its shape like a cow,
with a white body and four horns,
its hair like a thatched raincoat,
its name is Àoyín,
and it eats people.
There is a bird,
with one head and three bodies,
its shape like a pheasant,
its name is Chī.
Another one hundred and ninety *lǐ* to the west,
is called Guī Shān,
on which there is much jade but no stone.
The god Qítóng dwells there,
its sound is constantly like bells and chimes.
Below it are many accumulated snakes.
Another three hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the west,
is called Tiān Shān,
which has much gold and jade,
and blue realgar.
The Yīng River issues from it,
and flows southwest, emptying into Tāng Valley.
There is a god,
its shape like a yellow sack,
As red as cinnabar fire,
with six feet and four wings,
a featureless, shapeless mass,
this one is skilled at singing and dancing,
it is indeed Dì Jiāng.
Two hundred and ninety *lǐ* further west,
is called Yǒushān Mountain,
where the deity Rùshōu resides.
On its top there is much *yīng duǎn* jade,
on its sunny side there is much *jǐn yú* jade,
on its shady side there is much blue realgar.
This mountain is the place,
from which one can see the setting sun to the west;
its *qì* is round.
It is overseen by the deity of red light.
A hundred *lǐ* of water flowing west,
reaches Yìwàng Mountain,
where there is no grass or trees,
but much metal and jade.
There is a beast there,
which looks like a *lí* (leopard cat),
with one eye and three tails,
named Huān.
Its sound is like the capture of a hundred voices;
it can be used to ward off misfortune.
Wearing it cures jaundice.
There is a bird there,
which looks like a crow,
It has three heads and six tails, and it is good at laughing.
Its name is Qítú 鵸鵌.
Wearing it makes one unhated.
Moreover, it can ward off evil.
In general, the beginning of the *Classic of the Western Mountains, Third Sequence*
from Mount Chóngwú 崇吾之山 to Mount Yìwàng 翼望之山,
comprises a total of twenty-three mountains,
spanning six thousand seven hundred forty-four *lǐ*.
The forms of their spirits are all sheep bodies with human faces.
The ritual for their worship
involves burying one auspicious jade,
with offerings of millet.
The beginning of the *Classic of the Western Mountains, Fourth Sequence* is called Mount Yīn 陰山,
which has much paper mulberry on top.
It has no rocks.
Its grass is mostly flourishing thatch.
The Yīn River 陰水 originates here
and flows west to empty into the Luo River 洛.
Fifty *lǐ* to the north is
Mount Láo 勞山,
which has much gromwell.
The Ruò River 弱水 originates here
and flows west to empty into the Luo River 洛.
Fifty *lǐ* to the west is
It is called Bàgǔ zhī Shān (罷谷之山). The Ěr Shuǐ (洱水) originates here,
and flows west, emptying into the Luò (洛).
There are many purple and green stones within it.
One hundred and seventy *lǐ* to the north,
is called Shēn Shān (申山).
On its summit, there are many *gǔ* (榖) and *zuò* (柞) trees,
and below, there are many *niǔ* (杻) and *jiāng* (橿) trees.
On its sunny side, there are abundant gold and jade.
The Qū Shuǐ (區水) originates here,
and flows east, emptying into the Hé (河).
Two hundred *lǐ* to the north,
is called Niǎo Shān (鳥山).
On its summit, there are many mulberry trees,
and below, there are many paper mulberry trees.
On its shady side, there is abundant iron,
and on its sunny side, there is abundant jade.
The Rù Shuǐ (辱水) originates here,
and flows east, emptying into the Hé (河).
Again, one hundred and twenty *lǐ* to the north,
is called Shàng Shēn zhī Shān (上申之山).
There are no grasses or trees on its summit,
but there are many gravelly rocks.
Below, there are many hazel and *hù* (楛) trees,
and the beasts are mostly white deer.
The birds are mostly *dānghù* (當扈),
which look like pheasants,
Because its beard flies,
eating it doesn't cause one to blink.
Tāng River emerges from it,
flowing eastward and emptying into the Yellow River.
Again, 180 *lǐ* to the north,
is called Zhūcì Mountain.
Zhūcì River emerges from it,
flowing eastward and emptying into the Yellow River.
This mountain,
has much wood but no grass.
Birds and beasts do not dwell there.
It has many snakes.
Again, 180 *lǐ* to the north,
is called Hào Mountain.
Its trees are mostly lacquer trees and palm trees,
its grass is mostly *yào*, *xiāo*, and *xiōngqióng*. It has much *gānhán* stone.
Duān River emerges from it,
flowing eastward and emptying into the Yellow River.
Again, 220 *lǐ* to the north,
is called Yú Mountain.
Its northern slope has much iron,
its southern slope has much copper.
Its beasts are mostly white wolves and white tigers,
its birds are mostly white pheasants and white long-tailed pheasants.
Shēng River emerges from it,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Two hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the west,
is called Bái Yú zhī Shān,
its upper slopes abound with pines and cypresses,
its lower slopes abound with oaks and sandalwood;
its beasts are mostly yak and *xiányáng*,
its birds are mostly owls.
The Luò River originates on its sunny (south-facing) side,
and flows eastward into the Wei River;
the Jiá River originates on its shady (north-facing) side,
and flows eastward into the Shēng River.
Three hundred *lǐ* northwest,
is called Yóushǒu zhī Shān,
without grass or trees,
with snow in winter and summer.
The Shēn River originates on its top,
and flows hidden beneath its base,
it is rich in white jade.
Again, fifty-five *lǐ* to the west,
is called Jīnggǔ zhī Shān,
from which the Jīng River originates,
flowing southeastward into the Wei River,
it is rich in white gold and white jade.
Again, one hundred and twenty *lǐ* to the west,
is called Gāng Shān,
There is much qī wood, much
qióngfú jade.
The Gāng River originates here,
flowing north and emptying into the Wèi River.
Here, there are many gods called xī,
whose appearance is that of a human face with the body of a beast,
with one foot and one hand,
and their sound is like that of a qīn musical instrument.
Two hundred li further west,
one arrives at the tail of Gāng Mountain.
The Luò River originates here,
and flows north, emptying into the Yellow River.
Within it, there are many mánmán,
whose appearance is that of a rat's body with a turtle's head,
and their sound is like the barking of a dog.
Three hundred and fifty li further west,
is a mountain called Yīngdī.
On the upper part, there is much lacquer wood,
and on the lower part, there is much gold and jade.
The birds and beasts are entirely white.
The Yuàn River originates here,
and flows north, emptying into the Lingyang Marsh.
Here, there are many Rǎnyí fish,
with the body of a fish and the head of a snake,
and six feet.
Their eyes are like the ears of a horse,
Eating it will prevent one from being drowsy;
it can ward off misfortune.
Another three hundred *lǐ* to the west
is called Mount Zhōngqū.
Its southern slope has much jade;
its northern slope has much realgar, white jade, and gold.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a horse but with a white body and a black tail,
with one horn,
tiger teeth and claws,
its sound is like the sound of a drum.
Its name is Bó;
it eats tigers and leopards;
it can ward off weapons.
There is a tree there,
its appearance is like a táng tree,
with round leaves and red fruit,
the fruit is as large as a quince;
its name is Huái tree;
eating it gives one strength.
Another two hundred and sixty *lǐ* to the west
is called Mount Guī.
On it there is a beast,
its appearance is like a cow,
with hedgehog-like fur,
its name is Qióngqí;
its sound is like a háogǒu dog,
It is a man-eater. The Méng River originates here,
flowing south and emptying into the Yáng River.
There are many yellow cowries within it.
(There is the) Luó fish,
which has the body of a fish but the wings of a bird,
and makes a sound like yuānyāng (mandarin ducks).
When it appears, that town will have a great flood.
Two hundred and twenty *lǐ* further west is
the mountain called Niǎo Shǔ Tóng Xué zhī Shān (Bird-Rat Shared Hole Mountain).
It has many white tigers and white jade on it.
The Wèi River originates here,
and flows eastward, emptying into the Yellow River.
There are many sāo fish within it.
They look like zhān fish;
when they move excessively, that town will have a great war.
The water originates on its west side,
flowing west and emptying into the Hàn River.
There are many fú pí fish;
they look like overturned cooking pots,
with the head of a bird, and the wings and tail of a fish.
Their sound is like that of a qìng stone.
They produce pearls and jade.
Three hundred and sixty *lǐ* southwest is
the mountain called Yān Zī zhī Shān.
It has many red trees (dānmù) on it.
Their leaves are like those of the 榖 (gǔ) tree. Its
The fruit is as large as a melon,
with red markings and black veins.
Eating it cures jaundice
and can ward off fire.
Its sunny side has many turtles;
its shady side has much jade.
The Tiáo River (Tiáo Shuǐ) originates here
and flows westward into the sea,
where many whetstones are found.
There is a beast here,
with the body of a horse and the wings of a bird,
a human face and a snake's tail.
It delights in lifting people up;
its name is Shúhú (孰湖).
There is a bird here,
resembling an owl but with a human face,
the body of a long-tailed macaque and a dog's tail.
Its cry is like calling its own name.
Its appearance forebodes great drought in the region.
In total, the *Classic of the Mountains: West, Section Four,* from the Yīn Mountain (Yīn Shān) downward
to the Ēnzī Mountain (Ēnzī zhī Shān),
includes nineteen mountains,
spanning three thousand six hundred eighty *lǐ*.
The sacrificial rites for their deities
all use a single white chicken for prayer.
The offerings consist of unhusked rice
and white rushes as mats.
The mountains of the *Xī Jīng* (西經, Western Classic), to the right,
number seventy-seven in all,
spanning seventeen thousand five hundred and seventeen *lǐ*.
The Third Classic of the *Běi Shān Jīng* (北山經, Classic of the Northern Mountains)
begins with
Dānhú zhī Shān (單狐之山, Mount Dānhú),
which has an abundance of *jī* wood,
and its summit is covered with flowering grasses.
The Féng River (漨水) originates here
and flows westward into the Yóu River (泑水),
which contains abundant *zǐ* stone and patterned stone.
Two hundred and fifty *lǐ* further north
lies Qiúrú zhī Shān (求如之山, Mount Qiúrú),
which has an abundance of copper on its summit
and jade below,
devoid of grass and trees.
The Huá River (滑水) originates here
and flows westward into the Zhūpí River (諸毗之水).
It contains abundant *huá* fish,
which resemble eels,
with red backs,
and make a sound like *wú*.
Eating them cures warty growths.
It contains abundant water horses,
which resemble horses,
It has patterned arms and an ox's tail;
its sound is like calling out.
Three hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Dài Shān,
on which there is much jade,
and below which there is much cyan jasper.
There is a beast,
its shape is like a horse,
with a single horn with a rasp-like texture,
its name is Tuíshū,
which can ward off fire.
There is a bird,
its shape is like a crow,
with five colors and red markings,
its name is Qítú;
it reproduces by itself, without needing a mate;
eating it will prevent carbuncles.
The Péng River originates here,
and flows west to empty into the water of the Bì Lake,
in which there are many shū fish,
its shape is like a chicken but with
red feathers,
three tails, six feet, and four eyes;
its sound is like a magpie;
eating it can cure worry.
Four hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Qiáo Míng zhī Shān,
The Qiáo River springs forth here,
flowing westward and emptying into the Yellow River.
Within it are many Héluó fish,
with one head and ten bodies,
whose sound is like a barking dog;
eating it can cure carbuncles.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a raccoon dog with red bristles,
its sound is like "liú liú,"
named Mènghuái,
which can ward off misfortune.
This mountain,
has no grasses or trees,
and is rich in qīng xiónghuáng (a type of mineral pigment).
Three hundred and fifty li further north,
is Zhuōguāng Mountain,
from which the Xiāo River springs,
flowing westward and emptying into the Yellow River.
Within it are many Xíxí fish,
their appearance is like magpies but with ten wings,
their scales are all at the ends of their feathers,
their sound is like magpies,
they can ward off fire,
eating them prevents dān (a type of skin disease).
Its top has many pines and cypresses,
its lower slopes have many zōng jiāng (types of trees),
the beasts there are mostly língyáng (antelopes),
the birds are mostly fān (a type of bird).
Again, 380 *lǐ* further north,
is called Mount Guó (Guó Shān).
On its summit there is much lacquer,
below, there are many *tóng* and *jū* trees,
on its sunny (south-facing) side, there is much jade,
on its shady (north-facing) side, there is much iron.
The Yī River (Yī Shuǐ) rises here,
and flows westward into the Yellow River (Hé).
Among the beasts, there are many Bactrian camels (*tuótuo*),
among the birds, there are many *yù*,
which look like rats but have birds’ wings,
their sound is like sheep,
and they can ward off weapons.
Again, 400 *lǐ* further north,
reaching the tail end of Mount Guó (Guó Shān),
on its summit there is much jade but no stone.
The Yú River (Yú Shuǐ) rises here,
and flows westward into the Yellow River (Hé),
in it there are many patterned shells (*wénbèi*).
Again, 200 *lǐ* further north,
is called Mount Dānxūn (Dānxūn Zhī Shān),
on its summit there are many ailanthus and cypress trees,
among its plants, there are many chives and garlic,
and much cinnabar.
The Xūn River (Xūn Shuǐ) rises here,
and flows westward into the Táng River (Táng Shuǐ).
There is a beast, its appearance is like a rat,
but with a rabbit's head and deer's ears.
Its cry is like that of a háo dog.
It flies using its tail.
It is named Ěrshǔ.
Eating it can prevent boils,
and it can also ward off a hundred poisons.
Two hundred and eighty *lǐ* further north,
there is a mountain called Shízhě zhī Shān.
There is no grass or trees on it,
and it is abundant in jade and blue-green stones.
The Cǐ River originates from here
and flows west into the Hé River.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a leopard,
with patterned forehead and white body.
It is named Mèngjí.
It is good at hiding,
and its cry is like calling its own name.
One hundred and ten *lǐ* further north,
there is a mountain called Biānchūn zhī Shān, abundant
in onions, peaches, mallows, chives, and plums.
The Gàng River originates from here
and flows west into the Yòuzé swamp.
There is a beast,
Its appearance is like that of a *yú* 禺 and it has a tattooed body.
It is good at laughing.
When it sees people, it lies down.
Its name is Yōu'ān 幽鴳.
Its cry is its own name.
Two hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Mount Mànlián 蔓聯.
On it there are no grasses or trees.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like that of a *yú* 禺 but it has a mane.
It has the tail of an ox, tattooed arms, and horse hooves.
When it sees people, it laughs.
Its name is Zúzī 足訾.
Its cry is its own name.
There is a bird there,
which lives in groups and flies in flocks.
Its feathers are like those of a female pheasant.
Its name is Jiāo 鵁.
Its cry is its own name.
Eating it cures wind-related illnesses.
One hundred and eighty *lǐ* further north,
is called Mount Dānzhāng 單張.
On it there are no grasses or trees.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like that of a leopard but with a long tail,
a human head and ox ears,
A single-eyed beast,
named Zhūjiān 諸犍,
good at roaring.
When it moves, it holds its tail in its mouth;
when it rests, it coils its tail around itself.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like a pheasant,
but with a patterned head, white wings, and yellow feet,
named Báiyè 白鵺.
Eating it can cure throat pain,
and can also cure skin diseases.
The Lìshuǐ 櫟水 River originates here,
and flows south into the Gàngshuǐ 杠水 River.
Again, 320 *lǐ* to the north,
is called Mount Guàntí 灌題之山.
On it grow many ailanthus and *zhe* trees;
below it are many quicksands,
and many whetstones.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like an ox but with a white tail,
its sound is like the bellowing of cattle, named
Nàfǔ 那父.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like a female pheasant but with a human face,
when it sees people, it jumps,
named Sǒngsī 竦斯,
its cry is like its own name.
The Jiàng Hán River originates there,
and flows westward into the Yǒu Marsh,
which contains a lot of lodestone.
Two hundred *lǐ* further north
is called Pān Hóu Mountain.
The top of it has a lot of pines and cypresses,
and the bottom of it has a lot of hazel and *hù* trees.
Its southern side has a lot of jade,
and its northern side has a lot of iron.
There is an animal there
which looks like a cow,
and it has hair growing from its four joints,
named the máo niú (yak).
The Biān River originates there,
and flows south into the Lì Marsh.
Two hundred and thirty *lǐ* further north
is called Xiǎo Xián Mountain.
There are no grasses or trees,
and there is snow in winter and summer.
Two hundred and eighty *lǐ* further north
is called Dà Xián Mountain.
There are no grasses or trees,
and below it there is a lot of jade.
This mountain is square,
and cannot be climbed.
There is a snake called cháng shé (long snake)
Its fur is like a pig's bristles,
its sound is like a drum and clapper.
Three hundred and twenty *lǐ* further north,
is called Dūnhōng zhī Shān (敦薨之山).
On it are many palm and nán trees,
below it are many purple gromwell plants.
The Dūnhōng zhī Shuǐ (敦薨之水) rises here,
and flows westward into the Yǒuzé Marsh (泑澤).
It originates from the northeast corner of the Kūnlún (崑崙) Mountains,
and is actually the source of the [Yellow] River.
In it are many red salmon.
Among the animals are many rhinoceros and yaks;
among the birds are many turtle doves.
Two hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Shǎo Xián zhī Shān (少咸之山).
There are no grasses or trees;
there is much green jade.
There is an animal,
its shape is like a cow,
but with a red body, a human face, and horse hooves.
Its name is Yàyǔ (窫窳),
its sound is like that of a baby.
It eats people.
The Dūn River (敦水) rises here,
and flows eastward into the Yànmén zhī Shuǐ (鴈門之水).
In it are many yún yú (䰽䰽之魚),
eating them kills people.
Further north for two hundred *lǐ*,
is called Yùfǎ zhī Shān (獄法之山).
The Huàizé zhī Shuǐ (瀤澤之水) originates here,
and flows northeast into the Tàizé (泰澤).
Within it are many yú yú (䲃魚),
their shape is like a carp but with chicken feet,
eating it cures warts.
There is a beast,
its shape is like a dog but with a human face,
good at throwing,
when it sees people, it laughs,
its name is Shānxiāo (山𤟤),
its movement is like the wind,
when it appears, the world experiences great winds.
Further north for one hundred *lǐ*,
is called Běiyuè zhī Shān (北嶽之山),
with many thorny jujubes and strong wood.
There is a beast,
its shape is like an ox
with four horns, human eyes, and pig ears,
its name is Zhūhuái (諸懷),
its sound is like a honking goose,
it eats people.
The Zhūhuái zhī Shuǐ (諸懷之水) originates here,
and flows west into the Xiāo Shuǐ (囂水),
within it are many yú yú (鮨魚),
with a fish body and a dog's head,
Its cry is like that of an infant;
eating it will cure madness.
Another one hundred and eighty *lǐ* to the north is
Mount Húnxī,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in copper and jade.
The Xiāo River originates here
and flows northwestward into the sea.
There is a snake with one head and two bodies,
named Féiyí;
its appearance portends a great drought in the country.
Another fifty *lǐ* to the north is
Mount Běidān,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in scallions and chives.
Another one hundred *lǐ* to the north is
Mount Píchā,
devoid of grass and trees,
and abundant in horses.
Another one hundred and eighty *lǐ* to the north is
Mount Běixiān,
where horses abound.
The Xiān River originates here
and flows northwestward into the Túwú River.
Another one hundred and seventy *lǐ* to the north is
Mount Dī,
abundant in horses.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a leopard but with a patterned head,
its name is Yǎo. The Dī
River originates here,
and flows eastward, emptying into the Tài Marsh,
in which there are many dragon-turtles.
In general, the beginning of the "Classic of the Northern Mountains,"
from Dānhú Mountain to Dī Mountain,
comprises twenty-five mountains,
spanning five thousand four hundred and ninety lǐ.
Their deities all have human faces and snake bodies.
To sacrifice to them,
a male chicken and a pig are buried as offerings,
and a guī tablet of auspicious jade is used,
To bury without offering sacrificial grain.
The people north of this mountain
all eat raw, uncooked things.
The beginning of the second section of the Northern Classic,
is east of the Hé River,
its peak resting on the Fén River,
and its name is Guǎn Cén Mountain.
On it there are no trees but much grass,
and below it, much jade.
The Fén River originates here,
and flows westward into the Hé River.
Further north for two hundred and fifty *lǐ*,
is Shǎoyáng Mountain.
On it is much jade,
and below it, much red silver.
The Suān River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Fén River,
in which there is much beautiful red ochre.
Further north for fifty *lǐ*,
is Xuányōng Mountain.
On it is much jade,
and below it, much copper.
Among its animals are many *lǘ* deer and *mí* deer,
among its birds are many white *dí* pheasants and white *jiū* birds.
The Jìn River originates here,
and flows southeastward into the Fén River.
In it are many *cí* fish,
Its appearance is like a *tiáo* fish, but with red scales.
Its sound is like scolding.
Eating it prevents arrogance.
Another two hundred *lǐ* to the north
is called Mount Húqí,
without grass or trees,
but with an abundance of green jade.
The Shèng River originates here
and flows northeastward into the Fén River,
where there is much cyan jade.
Another three hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the north
is called Mount Báishā,
three hundred *lǐ* in extent,
entirely sand,
with no grass, trees, birds, or beasts.
The Wěi River originates above it,
disappears beneath it,
and there is much white jade.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the north
is called Mount Ěrshì,
with no grass or trees,
and no water.
Another three hundred and eighty *lǐ* to the north
is called Mount Kuáng,
with no grass or trees.
This is the mountain,
with snow in winter and summer.
A turbulent stream emerges from it,
flowing westward into the Fú River,
which contains much beautiful jade.
Further north for three hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
is called Zhūyú zhī Shān,
on which there is much copper and jade,
and below which there are many pines and cypresses.
The Zhūyú River rises from it,
flowing eastward into the Máo River.
Further north for three hundred and fifty *lǐ*,
is called Dūntóu zhī Shān,
on which there is much gold and jade,
but no vegetation.
The Máo River rises from it,
flowing eastward into the Qióng Marsh,
which contains many *xié* horses,
with ox tails and white bodies,
and one horn
whose sound is like calling out.
Further north for three hundred and fifty *lǐ*,
is called Gōuwú zhī Shān,
on which there is much jade,
and below which there is much copper.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a sheep's body with a human face,
its eyes are under its armpits,
tiger teeth and human claws,
its voice is like that of an infant,
its name is Páo Xiāo,
it eats people.
Three hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called the Mountain of Běi Xiāo,
without stones,
its south side has much *bì* (a type of blue or green jade),
its north side has much jade.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a tiger,
but with a white body and a dog's head,
a horse's tail and boar's bristles,
its name is Dú Gū.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like a crow,
with a human face,
its name is Jiāo Lì,
it flies at night and hides during the day,
eating it will cure heatstroke.
The Cén River originates here,
and flows eastward into Qióng Marsh.
Three hundred and fifty *lǐ* further north,
is called the Mountain of Liáng Qú,
without grass or trees,
It has much gold and jade.
The Xiū River (Xiū Shuǐ) originates here,
and flows east to pour into Yànmén.
Its animals are mostly Jūjì,
which look like hedgehogs (huì) with red fur,
and sound like piglets.
There is a bird,
which looks like a Kuāfù,
with four wings, one eye, and a dog's tail,
named Xiāo,
and sounds like a magpie.
Eating it will cure stomachaches,
and can stop bleeding.
Again, 400 *lǐ* to the north,
is called Mount Gūguàn,
which has no grass or trees.
On this mountain,
there is snow in winter and summer.
Again, 380 *lǐ* to the north,
is called Mount Húguàn.
On its south side (yáng), there is much jade,
and on its north side (yīn), there is much green jasper.
There are many horses.
The Húguàn River originates here,
and flows east to pour into the sea.
In it are many [䱇] (unknown fish).
There is a tree,
Its leaves are like willow leaves but with red veins.
Further north, traveling five hundred *lǐ* by water,
and three hundred *lǐ* through quicksand,
one arrives at Huán Shān,
where there is much gold and jade.
Three mulberry trees grow there.
All its trees have no branches.
They are a hundred *rèn* tall.
A hundred fruit trees grow there.
Below them are many strange snakes.
Further north, three hundred *lǐ*,
is a mountain called Dūn Tí Zhī Shān.
There is no grass or trees.
There is much gold and jade.
This is the *chún yú* of the North Sea.
In total, the beginning of the *Běi Cì Èr Jīng* (Second Classic of the North),
from Guǎn Cén Zhī Shān to Dūn Tí Zhī Shān,
consists of seventeen mountains in total,
spanning five thousand six hundred and ninety *lǐ*.
Their deities all have snake bodies and human faces.
Their sacrifices:
the offerings are one male chicken and a pig buried;
one *bì* and one *guī* are used,
thrown in without rice.
The beginning of the *Běi Cì Sān Jīng* (Third Classic of the North) is called Tài Háng Zhī Shān.
Its first mountain is called Guī Shān,
On it are gold and jade,
and beneath it is lapis lazuli.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a língyáng (antelope) but with four horns,
a horse's tail and spurs,
its name is Tuí,
it is good at dodging,
its cry sounds like jiào.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a magpie,
with a white body, red tail, and six feet,
its name is Qiú,
it is easily startled,
its cry sounds like xiāo.
Another two hundred *lǐ* northeast,
is called Lónghóu zhī Shān (Mount Dragon Marquis),
without grass or trees,
abundant in gold and jade.
The Jué River originates here,
and flows east into the Yellow River.
Within it are many "people-fish,"
their appearance is like the Zhuān fish,
with four feet,
their sound is like that of an infant,
eating it prevents foolish diseases.
Another two hundred *lǐ* northeast,
is called Mǎchéng zhī Shān (Mount Horse Completion),
on it are many patterned stones,
Its shady side has much gold and jade.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a white dog with a black head,
it flies when it sees people,
its name is Tiānmǎ (天馬),
its cry is like self-scolding.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a crow,
with a white head and a blue body, and yellow feet,
it is named Qūjū (鶌鶋),
its cry is like self-mockery,
eating it will prevent hunger,
and can cure goiter.
Seventy *lǐ* further northeast,
is called Xián Shān (咸山),
on it there is jade,
and below it there is much copper,
there are many pine and cypress trees,
the grass is mostly purple gromwell.
The Tiáojiān River (條菅之水) originates from here,
and flows southwest into the Chángzé (長澤) Marsh.
In it there is much *qìsuān*,
which forms once every three years,
eating it will cure leprosy.
Two hundred *lǐ* further northeast,
is called Tiānchí zhī Shān (天池之山),
on it there are no grasses or trees,
Duō Wénshí.
There is a beast,
it looks like a rabbit with the head of a rat,
and flies on its back.
Its name is Fēishǔ (flying squirrel).
The Miǎn River originates here,
flowing hidden beneath it,
and within it there is much yellow chalk.
Further east three hundred *lǐ*,
is called Yáng Shān.
Upon it is much jade,
and beneath it is much gold and copper.
There is a beast,
it looks like an ox but with a red tail,
its neck is humped,
its shape is like a bent halberd,
its name is Lǐnghú,
its cry is like "xiāo" (詨).
Eating it cures madness.
There is a bird,
it looks like a female pheasant,
and is patterned with five colors.
It is both male and female in itself,
and is named Xiàngshé.
Its cry is like "xiāo" (詨).
The Liú River originates here,
and flows south into the Yellow River.
Within it is the Chánfǔ fish,
Its form is like a crucian carp,
with the head of a fish but the body of a pig.
Eating it will stop vomiting.
Further east for 350 *lǐ*
is called Bēn Wén zhī Shān 賁聞之山.
Its top has much azure jade,
and its bottom has much yellow chalk,
and much niè stone.
Further north for 100 *lǐ*,
is called Wáng Wū zhī Shān 王屋之山,
where there is much stone.
The Yì Shuǐ 㶌水 rises here
and flows northwest to pour into the Tài Zé 泰澤.
Further northeast for 300 *lǐ*,
is called Jiāo Shān 教山.
Its top has much jade but no stone.
The Jiāo Shuǐ 教水 rises here,
and flows west to pour into the Hé 河 (Yellow River).
This water dries up in winter and flows in summer,
and is in reality a dry river.
Within it are two mountains,
these mountains,
are 300 *bù* in circumference.
Their name is Fā Wán zhī Shān 發丸之山,
and on them there is gold and jade.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Mount Jǐng (景山).
To the south, it overlooks the Yánfàn Marsh (鹽販之澤),
and to the north, it overlooks the Shǎo Marsh (少澤).
On it grow abundantly grasses and sweet potatoes.
Among the grasses, there is much *qínjiāo* (秦椒).
On its shady side, there is much ochre,
and on its sunny side, there is much jade.
There is a bird,
which looks like a snake,
but has four wings, six eyes, and three feet.
It is called Suānyú (酸與).
Its call is like itself,
and when it appears, there will be fear in that settlement.
Three hundred and twenty *lǐ* further southeast,
is called Mount Mèngmén (孟門之山).
On it grows abundant green jade,
and much metal; below it, there is much yellow clay
and much *nièshí* (涅石).
Three hundred and twenty *lǐ* further southeast,
is called Mount Píng (平山).
The Píng River (平水) originates on it,
and flows underground beneath it,
and there is abundant beautiful jade there.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east is called Mount Jīng (京山).
There is beautiful jade there,
It has much lacquered wood,
much bamboo.
On its sunny side is red copper,
on its shady side is dark-colored lodestone.
The Gāo River originates here,
and flows south to empty into the Hé River.
Two hundred *lǐ* further east is
Chóngwěi Mountain.
Its top has much gold and jade,
its base has much bamboo,
and much lapis lazuli.
The Dān River originates here,
and flows south to empty into the Hé River.
The Bó River originates here,
and flows southeast to empty into the Huángzé Marsh.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east is
Péngpí Mountain.
Its top has no grass or trees,
but much gold and jade;
its base has much water.
The Zǎolín River originates here,
and flows southeast to empty into the Hé River.
The Féi River originates here,
and flows south to empty into the Chuáng River,
where there are many Féiyí snakes.
Further east for 180 *lǐ*,
is called Mount Xiǎohóu.
The Míngzhāng River originates here,
and flows south into the Yellow Marsh.
There is a bird,
which looks like a crow but has white markings,
and is called the gūyú.
Eating it will prevent drowning.
Further east for 370 *lǐ*,
is called Mount Tàitóu.
The Gòng River originates here,
and flows south into Lake Hū.
Its upper part has much gold and jade,
and its lower part has much bamboo for arrows.
Further northeast for 200 *lǐ*,
is called Mount Xuānyuán.
Its upper part has much copper,
and its lower part has much bamboo.
There is a bird,
which looks like an owl but has a white head,
and its name is huángniǎo.
Its cry sounds like "zì xiāo",
and eating it will prevent jealousy.
Further north for 200 *lǐ*,
is called Mount Yèlì.
Its upper part has many pines and cypresses,
There is gold and jade.
The Qìn Shuǐ (沁水) originates here,
flowing south to empty into the Hé (河, Yellow River).
To its east is a forest,
named Dān Lín (丹林).
The waters of Dān Lín (丹林) originate here,
flowing south to empty into the Hé (河, Yellow River).
The Yīng Hóu (嬰侯) River originates here,
flowing north to empty into the Fàn Shuǐ (氾水).
Three hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is called Jǔ Rù zhī Shān (沮洳之山).
There are no grasses or trees,
but there is gold and jade.
The Qí Shuǐ (濝水) originates here,
flowing south to empty into the Hé (河, Yellow River).
Again, three hundred *lǐ* to the north,
is called Shén Qūn zhī Shān (神囷之山).
On its summit are patterned stones,
and beneath it are white snakes,
and flying insects.
The Huáng Shuǐ (黃水) originates here,
and flows east to empty into the Huán (洹) River.
The Fù Shuǐ (滏水) originates here,
and flows east to empty into the Ōu Shuǐ (歐水).
Again, two hundred *lǐ* to the north,
It is called Fājiū Mountain,
on which there are many Zhe trees.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like a crow,
with patterned head, white beak, and red feet,
its name is Jīngwèi,
its cry sounds like "zì xiāo".
It is the young daughter of Yándì, named Nǚwā.
Nǚwā was playing in the East Sea,
drowned and did not return,
therefore she became Jīngwèi,
constantly carrying wood and stones from the Western Mountains,
in order to fill up the East Sea.
The Zhāng River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Again, 120 *lǐ* northeast of here,
is called Shǎo Mountain,
on which there are gold and jade,
and beneath which there is copper.
The Qīng Zhāng River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Zhuó Zhāng River.
Again, 200 *lǐ* northeast of here,
is called Xī Mountain,
on which there is much jade,
and beneath which there are whetstones.
The Niúshǒu River originates here,
And it flows eastward into the Fǔ Shuǐ (滏水).
Two hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Jǐng Shān (景山),
where there is fine jade.
The Jǐng Shuǐ (景水) originates here,
and flows southeast into the Hǎi Zé (海澤).
One hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Tíshǒu zhī Shān (題首之山),
where there is jade,
and many stones,
but no water.
One hundred *lǐ* further north,
is called Xiù Shān (繡山),
on which there is jade and azure jade.
Its trees are mostly *xún* trees (栒),
and its grasses are mostly peony and *xiōng qióng* (芎窮).
The Wěi Shuǐ (洧水) originates here,
and flows eastward into the Hé (河, Yellow River).
In it, there are *huò* (鱯) and *mǐn* (黽).
One hundred and twenty *lǐ* further north,
is called Sōng Shān (松山).
The Yáng Shuǐ (陽水) originates here,
and flows northeast into the Hé (河, Yellow River).
One hundred and twenty *lǐ* further north,
It is called Dūnyǔ zhī Shān 敦與之山.
On its top there are no grasses or trees,
but there are gold and jade.
The Suò Shuǐ 溹水 originates from its southern side,
and flows eastward, emptying into the Tài Lù zhī Shuǐ 泰陸之水.
The Zhī Shuǐ 泜水 originates from its northern side,
and flows eastward, emptying into the Péng Shuǐ 彭水.
The Huái Shuǐ 槐水 originates here,
and flows eastward, emptying into the Zhī Zé 泜澤.
Further north for one hundred and seventy *lǐ*,
it is called Zhè Shān 柘山.
On its southern side there are gold and jade,
and on its northern side there is iron.
The Lìjù zhī Shuǐ 歷聚之水 originates here,
and flows northward, emptying into the Wěi Shuǐ 洧水.
Further north for three hundred *lǐ*,
it is called Wéilóng zhī Shān 維龍之山.
On its top there is green jade,
on its southern side there is gold,
and on its northern side there is iron.
The Féi Shuǐ 肥水 originates here,
and flows eastward, emptying into the Gāo Zé 皋澤.
Within it there are many lěishí 礨石.
The Chǎngtiě zhī Shuǐ 敞鐵之水 originates here,
and flows northward, emptying into the Dà Zé 大澤.
Further north for one hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
It is called Báimǎ zhī Shān (白馬之山),
on its sunny side there are many stone jades,
on its shady side there is much iron,
and much red copper.
Mùmǎ zhī Shuǐ (木馬之水) originates here,
and flows northeast into the Hūtuó (虖沱).
Two hundred *lǐ* further north,
it is called Kōngsāng zhī Shān (空桑之山),
without grass or trees,
and having snow in winter and summer.
Dōngsāng zhī Shuǐ (冬桑之水) originates here,
and flows east into the Hūtuó (虖沱).
Three hundred *lǐ* further north,
it is called Tàixì zhī Shān (泰戲之山),
without grass or trees,
and with much gold and jade.
There is a beast there,
its shape is like a sheep,
with one horn and one eye,
the eye is behind the ear,
its name is Dùndùn (䍶䍶),
its cry is like shouting.
The Hūtuó zhī Shuǐ (虖沱之水) originates here,
and flows east into the Lóu Shuǐ (漊水).
Yènǚ zhī Shuǐ (液女之水) originates on its sunny side,
and flows south into the Qìn Shuǐ (沁水).
Going three hundred *lǐ* further north,
there is Shí Mountain,
which abounds in gold and jade.
The Huòhuò River originates here
and flows eastward into the Hūtuó River.
The Xiānyú River originates here
and flows southward into the Hūtuó River.
Going two hundred *lǐ* further north,
there is Tóngróng Mountain.
The Gāotú River originates here
and flows eastward into the Lóuyè River.
Going three hundred *lǐ* further north,
there is Gāoshì Mountain.
The Zī River originates here
and flows southward into the Hūtuó River.
Its trees are mostly palm trees,
and its grasses are mostly *tiáo* grasses.
The Kōu River originates here
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Going three hundred *lǐ* further north,
there is Lù Mountain,
which abounds in fine jade. The Qióng
River originates here
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Further north for two hundred *lǐ*,
is called Yí Shān.
The Bān River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
One hundred and twenty *lǐ* to the north,
is called Yān Shān;
it has many *yīng* stones.
The Yān River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Continuing north for five hundred *lǐ* over mountains,
and five hundred *lǐ* by water,
one arrives at Ráo Shān.
There is no vegetation here,
and many fine jades.
The beasts here are mostly Bactrian camels,
and the birds are mostly owls.
The Lì Guó River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River.
Within it are *shī* fish,
eating them will kill a person.
Further north for four hundred *lǐ*,
is called Qián Shān;
there is no vegetation,
its south side has gold and jade,
its north side has iron and no water.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like an ox but with three legs.
Its name is Yuán,
its cry sounds like xiāo.
Again, 500 li to the north is
Lún Mountain.
The Lún River originates there,
and flows east into the Yellow River.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a mí deer,
its zhōu (administrative division) is on its tail,
its name is Píjiǔ.
Again, 500 li to the north is
Mount Jiéshí.
The Shéng River originates there,
and flows east into the Yellow River,
in which there are many Púyí fish.
On top of it there is jade,
below it there is much qīngbì (lapis lazuli or similar blue-green stone).
Again, traveling 500 li by water to the north,
one arrives at Mount Yànmén,
where there is no grass or trees.
Again, traveling 400 li by water to the north,
one arrives at the Great Marsh (Tàizé).
Among them is a mountain,
called Dì Dū zhī Shān (帝都之山),
a hundred *lǐ* in extent,
without grass or trees,
but with gold and jade.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the north,
is called Chún yú Wú Féng zhī Shān (錞于毋逢之山).
Looking north, one can see Jī Hào zhī Shān (雞號之山),
whose wind is like a whirlwind;
looking west, one can see Yōu Dū zhī Shān (幽都之山),
from which the Yù Shuǐ (浴水) River originates.
There is a large snake there,
with a red head and white body,
its sound like a cow's moo.
If it appears, there will be a great drought in that region.
In general, the beginning of the "Third Classic of the North,"
from Tài Háng zhī Shān (太行之山) to Wú Féng zhī Shān (無逢之山),
encompasses forty-six mountains,
spanning twelve thousand three hundred and fifty *lǐ*.
The appearances of the deities are all with horse bodies and human faces,
numbering twenty deities.
To sacrifice to them,
one buries one *zǎo zhǐ* (藻茝).
Fourteen deities
have the appearance of pig bodies carrying jade.
To sacrifice to them,
All are jade,
not buried.
Their ten gods,
their shapes are all pig bodies with eight feet,
and snake tails.
To sacrifice to them,
all use one *bì* jade to bury.
In total, forty-four gods,
all use *tú xǔ* rice to sacrifice to them,
all of these do not eat cooked food.
The mountain record of the Right Northern Classic,
in total eighty-seven mountains,
twenty-three thousand two hundred and thirty *lǐ*.
