Eastern Mountain Classic, Fourth
The beginning of the *Dōng Shān Jīng*,
is called Sù Zōng Mountain,
north of it borders Qián Mèi.
The Shí River originates here,
and flows northeast into the sea.
Within it are many yōng yōng fish,
their shape is like a Li cattle,
their sound is like a pig squealing.
Again, three hundred *lǐ* to the south,
is called Lěi Mountain,
on it there is jade,
Below it there is gold.
Lake water emerges from here,
flowing eastward into the Shí River.
Within it are many huóshī.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south is
Mount Xúnzhuàng,
where there is much gold and jade above,
and much green-blue stone below.
There is a beast,
which looks like a dog,
with six feet.
Its name is Zōngzōng,
and its cry sounds like its own name.
There is a bird,
which looks like a chicken but has rat fur.
Its name is Yùshǔ,
and its appearance portends a great drought in that town.
The Yú River emerges from here,
and flows north into Lake Water.
Within it are many zhēnyú,
which look like chou fish,
with beaks like needles.
Eating it will prevent epidemic diseases.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south is
Mount Bózāi,
without grass or trees,
No water.
Another three hundred *lǐ* to the south is
Mount Fāntiáo,
where there are no grasses or trees,
but much sand.
The Jiǎn River originates here,
flowing north into the sea.
There are many *gǎn* fish in it.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the south is
Mount Gūér,
the top of which has much lacquer,
and the bottom has much mulberry and *zhè* trees.
The Gūér River originates here,
flowing north into the sea.
There are many *gǎn* fish in it.
Another four hundred *lǐ* to the south is
Mount Gāoshì,
the top of which has much jade,
and the bottom has much whetstone.
The Zhūshéng River originates here,
flowing east into a swamp.
There is much gold and jade in it.
Another three hundred *lǐ* to the south is
Mount Yuè,
On its heights grow many mulberry trees,
below grow many ailanthus trees.
The Luò River originates here,
flowing east and emptying into a marsh,
within which are many gold and jade.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Chái Shān,
on its heights there are no grasses or trees,
below there is much water,
within which are many Kānxù fish.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a Kuāfù but with pig bristles,
its sound is like shouting,
its appearance foretells a great flood throughout the land.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Dú Shān,
on its heights are many gold and jade,
below are many beautiful stones.
The Mòtú River originates here,
and flows southeast, emptying into the Miǎn River,
within which are many chīwěi,
their appearance is like yellow snakes,
with fish fins,
when they emerge and enter, there is light,
their appearance foretells a great drought in that settlement.
Again, 300 *lǐ* to the south,
is called Tài Shān.
On it, there is much jade,
and at its foot, there is much metal.
There is a beast,
its appearance is like a pig but it has pearls,
its name is called Tóngtóng,
its name is self-proclaimed.
The Huán River originates here,
flowing east and emptying into the Jiāng River,
within which there is much water jade.
Again, 300 *lǐ* to the south,
is called Zhú Shān,
adjoining the Jiāng River,
without grass or trees,
with much fine jade.
The Jī River originates here,
flowing southeast and emptying into the Qǔtán River,
within which there are many *zǐluǒ* (a type of shellfish).
In total, the beginning of the *Dōng Shān Jīng*,
from Sùsuǒ Mountain to Zhú Shān,
there are twelve mountains,
totaling 3600 *lǐ*.
The forms of the gods are all human bodies with dragon heads.
For sacrifices: the offering consists of one dog for prayer,
and the offering for *ní* consists of fish.
The first mountain of the *Dōng Cì Èr Jīng* (Eastern Second Classic)
is called Mount Kōngsāng,
which borders the Shí River to the north,
faces Jǔ Wú to the east,
faces Shālíng to the south, and
faces the Mǐn Marsh to the west.
There is a beast there,
which looks like an ox but has tiger stripes.
Its sound is like "qīn."
Its name is Línglíng,
and its cry is self-summoned.
Its appearance foretells a great flood in the world.
Furthermore, 600 *lǐ* to the south
is called Mount Cáoxī.
There are many grains below it, but no water.
There are many birds and beasts.
Furthermore, 400 *lǐ* to the southwest
is called Mount Yìgāo.
There are many gold and jades on it,
and much white clay below it.
The Yìgāo River originates there
and flows east, emptying into the Jī Nǚ River.
There are many *shèn* and *yáo* within it.
Furthermore, 500 *lǐ* of water travel to the south,
For three hundred *lǐ* through shifting sands,
one arrives at the tail of Mount Gé
, where there is no grass or trees,
and many whetstones.
Continuing south for three hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
one reaches the head of Mount Gé
, where there is no grass or trees.
The Lǐ River originates here,
flowing east to empty into Yú Marsh.
Within it are many pearl-shelled biē fish;
their appearance is like a lung, but with four eyes
and six legs, and possessing pearls.
Their taste is sour and sweet;
eating them prevents leprosy.
Continuing south for three hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
one reaches Mount Yú'é
, where the top has many catalpa and nan trees,
and the bottom has many thorny weeds and *qǐ* herbs.
The Záyú River originates here,
flowing east to empty into the Huáng River.
There is a beast
whose appearance is like a rabbit but with a bird's beak,
owl's eyes, and a snake's tail.
When it sees a person, it pretends to sleep.
It is named Gōu yú
, and its cry sounds like "*jiào*."
When it appears, locusts and grasshoppers will cause devastation.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
there is a mountain called Dùfǔ zhī Shān,
without grass or trees,
with abundant water.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
there is a mountain called Gěng Shān,
without grass or trees,
with abundant turquoise minerals,
and many large snakes.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a fox but with fish fins,
its name is called Zhū Nòu,
its cry is like calling its own name,
when it appears, the country will experience fear.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
there is a mountain called Lúqí zhī Shān,
without grass or trees,
with abundant sand and stones.
The Shā River originates from here,
flowing south into the Cén River,
in which there are many *díhú* birds,
their appearance is like mandarin ducks but with human feet,
their cry is like calling their own name,
when they appear, the country will have much earthwork construction.
Further south for three hundred and eighty *lǐ*,
is called Gūyè zhī Shān,
without grasses or trees,
abundant in water.
Further south, traveling by water for three hundred *lǐ*,
through a hundred *lǐ* of flowing sand,
is called Běi Gūyè zhī Shān,
without grasses or trees,
abundant in stones.
Further south for three hundred *lǐ*,
is called Nán Gūyè zhī Shān,
without grasses or trees,
abundant in water.
Further south for three hundred *lǐ*,
is called Bì Shān,
without grasses or trees,
abundant in large snakes,
abundant in *bìshuǐ* jade.
Further south for five hundred *lǐ*,
is called Gōushì zhī Shān,
without grasses or trees,
abundant in gold and jade.
The Yuán River originates here,
(It) flows east and empties into the Shāzé (沙澤) marsh.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Gūféng zhī Shān (姑逢之山),
(it) has no grass or trees,
(but) has much gold and jade.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a fox but with wings,
its sound is like a swan goose,
its name is Bìbì (獙獙),
(its) appearance portends great drought under Heaven.
Five hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Fúlì zhī Shān (鳧麗之山),
its top has much gold and jade,
its base has much *zhēn* stone.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a fox,
but (with) nine tails,
nine heads,
(and) tiger claws,
its name is Lóngzhì (蠪蛭),
its sound is like an infant,
this (beast) eats people.
Five hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Guī Shān (䃌山),
(it) faces south towards the Guī Shuǐ (䃌水),
Looking east, there are lakes and marshes.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a horse,
but with sheep's eyes,
four horns,
and an ox's tail.
Its sound is like that of a háogǒu (a type of wild dog).
Its name is Yóuyóu,
its appearance portends many cunning merchants in that country.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a wild duck but with a rat's tail,
good at climbing trees.
Its name is Jié Gōu,
its appearance portends much pestilence in that country.
In general, the beginning of the "Second Classic of the Eastern Region,"
from Kōngsāng Mountain to Pī Mountain,
includes seventeen mountains,
spanning six thousand six hundred and forty li.
The appearance of its deities is all beast-bodied with human faces, bearing antlers.
Their sacrifices:
The animal offering is one chicken,
and a jade ring is buried.
Further, the beginning of the "Third Classic of the Eastern Region,"
is called Shīhú Mountain.
Looking north, one can see Yán Mountain,
its summit has an abundance of gold and jade,
Below it are many thorns.
There is an animal,
its shape is like a mi deer but with fish eyes,
its name is Yuānhú,
its cry is like self-scolding.
Further south by water for eight hundred *lǐ* is
Mount Qíshān.
Its trees are mostly peach and plum,
its animals are mostly tigers.
Further south by water for five hundred *lǐ* is
Mount Zhūgōu,
it has no grass or trees,
and much sand and stone.
This mountain,
is a hundred *lǐ* in circumference,
and has many mèi fish.
Further south by water for seven hundred *lǐ* is
Mount Zhōngfǔ,
it has no grass or trees,
and much sand.
Further east by water for a thousand *lǐ* is
Mount Húshè,
it has no grass or trees,
and much sand and stone.
Further south, traveling seven hundred *lǐ* by water,
is a mountain called Mèngzǐ zhī Shān 孟子之山.
Its trees are mostly catalpa and paulownia,
and there are many peach and plum trees.
Its grasses are mostly mushrooms and cattails,
and its animals are mostly elk and deer.
This mountain
is a hundred *lǐ* wide and round.
On it, there is a spring of water,
named Bìyáng 碧陽.
In it, there are many sturgeon and *weí* fish.
Further south, traveling five hundred *lǐ* by water,
is a flowing desert (Liúshā 流沙).
Traveling five hundred *lǐ*,
there is a mountain,
called Qǐzhǒng zhī Shān 跂踵之山.
It is two hundred *lǐ* wide and round,
with no grasses or trees.
There are large snakes,
and much jade on it.
There is a body of water there,
forty *lǐ* wide and round, and it all bubbles up.
Its name is Shēnzé 深澤.
In it, there are many sea turtles.
There is a fish there,
its shape is like a carp,
and six feet, bird's tail,
is named the Gé gé zhī yú fish,
its cry is its own call.
Again, traveling nine hundred *lǐ* south by water,
is called Zǔ yú zhī shān Mountain,
on it are grass and trees,
much gold and jade,
much ochre.
There is a beast,
its shape is like a cow but with a horse's tail,
named Jīng jīng,
its cry is its own call.
Again, traveling five hundred *lǐ* south by water,
a quicksand of three hundred *lǐ*,
one arrives at Wú gāo zhī shān Mountain,
looking south to the Yòu hǎi Sea,
looking east to the Fú mù tree,
no grass or trees,
much wind.
This mountain
is a hundred *lǐ* wide.
In general, the beginning of the "Third Classic of the East,"
from Shī hú zhī shān Mountain to Wú gāo zhī shān Mountain,
is nine mountains in all,
six thousand nine hundred *lǐ*.
The appearance of its gods is all human-bodied with sheep horns.
Their sacrifices:
use one male sheep,
and use millet for the rice.
These gods,
when they appear, will cause wind, rain, and water damage.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the "Fourth Eastern Classic,"
is called Běi Hào Zhī Shān (北號之山),
overlooking the North Sea.
There is a tree there,
its appearance is like a poplar,
with red flowers,
its fruit is like a jujube but without a pit,
its taste is sour and sweet,
eating it prevents malaria.
Shí Shuǐ (食水) River originates from there,
and flows northeast into the sea.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a wolf,
with a red head and rat eyes,
its sound is like a piglet,
its name is Gé Dàn (獦狚),
it eats people.
There is a bird there,
its appearance is like a chicken but with a white head,
rat feet and tiger claws,
its name is Qí Què (鬿雀),
They also eat people.
Three hundred *lǐ* further south,
is called Máo Shān.
There are no grasses or trees.
The Cāngtǐ River originates here
and flows west into the Zhǎn River.
Many xiū fish are found there.
Their shape is like a carp but with a large head.
Those who eat them will not develop warts.
Three hundred and twenty *lǐ* further south,
is called Dōngshǐ Mountain.
The top has abundant blue jade.
There is a tree,
its shape is like a poplar but with red veins.
Its sap is like blood,
and it bears no fruit.
Its name is qǐ,
and it can be used to medicate horses.
The Cǐ River originates here
and flows northeast into the sea.
Many beautiful shells are found there,
as well as many zǐ fish.
Their shape is like a crucian carp,
with one head and ten bodies.
Their odor is like *míwú* (Ligusticum sinense),
and eating them prevents flatulence.
Three hundred *lǐ* further to the southeast is
Nǚzhēng Zhī Shān (女烝之山),
which is devoid of grass and trees.
Shígāo water (石膏水) springs forth from it
and flows westward into the Gé river (鬲水).
Within it are many bó fish (薄魚).
They resemble sturgeon fish (鱣魚) but have only one eye.
Their sound is like *ōu*.
Their appearance portends a great drought in the world.
Two hundred *lǐ* further to the southeast is
Qīn Shān (欽山),
which is rich in gold and jade but has no rocks.
The Shī river (師水) springs forth from it
and flows northward into Gāozé Marsh (皋澤).
Within it are many xiū fish (鱃魚)
and many patterned shells.
There is a beast there;
its appearance is like a pig but it has tusks.
Its name is Dāngkāng (當康).
Its cry is its own name.
Its appearance portends a great abundance in the world.
Two hundred *lǐ* further to the southeast is
Zǐtóng Zhī Shān (子桐之山).
The Zǐtóng river (子桐之水) springs forth from it
and flows westward into Yúrú Marsh (餘如之澤).
Among them are many yú fish.
Their shape is like fish with bird wings.
Their appearance and disappearance are accompanied by light.
Their sound is like yuānyāng (鴛鴦, mandarin ducks).
Their appearance portends great drought in the world.
Two hundred li northeast of there is
called Yǎn Shān (剡山),
with abundant gold and jade.
There is a beast there,
its shape is like a pig with a human face,
yellow body and red tail.
Its name is Héyǔ (合窳),
its sound is like an infant.
This beast,
eats people,
and also eats insects and snakes.
Its appearance portends great floods in the world.
Two hundred li east of there is
called Tài Shān (太山),
with abundant gold, jade,
and zhēn trees.
There is a beast there,
its shape is like a cow with a white head,
one eye and a snake tail.
Its name is Fēi (蜚),
if it walks through water, the water dries up;
If written in running script (xíngcǎo), it dies;
if seen, a great plague will sweep the world.
The Gōu River originates here,
and flows north into the Láo River.
There are many xiū fish in it.
In all, the beginning of the "Fourth Eastern Classic,"
from Běihào Mountain to Dà Mountain,
includes eight mountains,
totaling one thousand seven hundred and twenty *lǐ*.
The above is the record of the mountains in the Eastern Classic,
a total of forty-six mountains,
spanning eighteen thousand eight hundred and sixty *lǐ*.
Central Mountain Classic, Fifth
The "Central Mountain Classic" begins with Bó Mountain,
called Gānzǎo Mountain.
The Gòng River originates here,
and flows west into the Yellow River.
On it, there are many niǔ trees;
below it, there is a grass,
with a sunflower stem and apricot leaves,
yellow flowers and pod-like fruit,
named tuò,
which can cure blurred vision.
There is a beast,
which looks like a yíng rat with patterned forehead,
Its name is Suǒ,
eating it cures goiter.
Twenty *lǐ* further east,
is called Lì'ér Zhī Shān.
On it grows abundant jiāng trees,
and abundant lì trees.
This tree,
has square stems and round leaves,
yellow flowers and is hairy,
its fruit is like the liàn fruit,
taking it makes one never forget.
Fifteen *lǐ* further east,
is called Qúzhū Zhī Shān,
on it grows abundant bamboo.
The Qúzhū River originates here,
and flows south into the Hé (Yellow River).
Within it are many háo fish,
which look like sturgeon,
with red beaks, red tails, and red fins,
eating it can cure white lichen.
Thirty-five *lǐ* further east,
is called Cōnglóng Zhī Shān,
within it are many large valleys,
and abundant white clay,
black, blue,
Huáng È.
Fifteen *lǐ* further east,
is called Wōshān Mountain.
Its summit abounds in red copper,
and its shady side abounds in iron.
Seventy *lǐ* further east,
is called Tuōhù zhī Shān Mountain.
There is a plant there,
its appearance is like sunflower leaves with red flowers,
with pods,
the pods are like palm pods,
named Zhíchǔ,
it can cure *shǔ* disease,
eating it will prevent blurred vision.
Twenty *lǐ* further east,
is called Jīnxīng zhī Shān Mountain.
It abounds in Tiān Yīng,
its appearance is like dragon bones,
it can cure *cuó* skin disease.
Seventy *lǐ* further east,
is called Tàiwēi zhī Shān Mountain.
Within it, there is a valley called Xiāogǔ Valley,
which abounds in iron.
Again, fifteen *lǐ* to the east,
is called Mount Jiānggǔ,
in which there is much red copper.
Again, one hundred and twenty *lǐ* to the east,
is called Mount Wúlín,
in which there is much *jiāncǎo* grass.
Again, thirty *lǐ* to the north,
is called Mount Niúshǒu.
There is a grass,
named Guǐcǎo,
its leaves are like sunflower and its stem is red,
its flower is like grain,
consuming it prevents worry.
The Láoshuǐ River originates here,
and flows west, emptying into the Yùshuǐ River.
Here are many flying fish,
their shape is like crucian carp,
eating them cures hemorrhoids.
Again, forty *lǐ* to the north,
is called Mount Huò,
its trees mostly consist of *gǔ*.
There is an animal,
its shape is like a wildcat,
but with a white tail and a mane,
named Fěifěi,
Nurturing it can cure worry.
Fifty-two *lǐ* further north is
Hé Gǔ zhī Shān 合谷之山 (Mount Hé Gǔ),
where many *zhān jí* 薝棘 grow.
Thirty-five *lǐ* further north is
Yīn Shān 陰山 (Mount Yīn),
abundant in whetstones
and patterned stones.
Little Water emanates from there,
within which are many *diāo táng* 彫棠 trees,
their leaves resembling elm leaves but square,
and their fruits like red beans.
Eating them cures deafness.
Four hundred *lǐ* further northeast is
Gǔ Dèng zhī Shān 鼓鐙之山 (Mount Gǔ Dèng),
abundant in red copper.
There is a grass
called Róng Cǎo 榮草 (Róng Grass),
its leaves like willow,
its root like chicken eggs.
Eating it cures wind-related ailments.
In total, the mountains of the Bó Shān 薄山 range,
from Gān Zǎo zhī Shān 甘棗之山 (Mount Gān Zǎo) to Gǔ Dèng zhī Shān 鼓鐙之山 (Mount Gǔ Dèng),
comprise fifteen mountains,
Six thousand six hundred and seventy *lǐ*.
*Lì’ér*,
is a grave mound.
Its sacrificial rites:
with animal offerings, the provisions of a *tàiláo* (grand offering consisting of an ox, a sheep, and a pig);
suspending *jí* jade.
As for the remaining thirteen mountains,
the animal offering uses one sheep,
suspending infant silk seals, using *sāngfēng*,
burying (the offering) without rice.
*Sāngfēng* are,
mulberry deities.
They are square at the bottom and pointed at the top,
with a hole in the middle, to which metal is added.
*Zhōng Cì Èr Jīng*: At the head of the *Jì* Mountains,
is called *Huīzhū* Mountain.
On it there is much mulberry,
its beasts are mostly *lǘmí* (deer-like animals),
its birds are mostly *hé* (pheasants).
Two hundred *lǐ* further southwest,
is called *Fāshì* Mountain.
On it there is much gold and jade,
at its base there is much whetstone.
The *Jíyú* River rises from it,
and flows west into the *Yī* River.
Further three hundred *lǐ* to the west,
is called Mount Háo (Háoshān).
On it there is much gold and jade but no grass or trees.
Further three hundred *lǐ* to the west,
is called Mount Xiān (Xiānshān).
There is much gold and jade,
and no grass or trees.
The Xiān River (Xiānshuǐ) originates here,
and flows north to empty into the Yī River (Yīshuǐ).
Within it are many Míng Snakes (Míngshé),
whose shape is like a snake but with four wings,
their sound is like a *qìng* chime,
and when they appear, their settlement will suffer a great drought.
Further three hundred *lǐ* to the west,
is called Mount Yáng (Yángshān).
There are many stones,
and no grass or trees.
The Yáng River (Yángshuǐ) originates here,
and flows north to empty into the Yī River (Yīshuǐ).
Within it are many Huà Snakes (Huàshé),
whose shape is like a human face but with a jackal's body,
bird wings, and snake-like movement,
their sound is like scolding and shouting,
and when they appear, their settlement will suffer a great flood.
Further two hundred *lǐ* to the west,
It is called Mount Kūnwú,
on which there is much red copper.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a pig but it has horns,
its cry is like a howl,
its name is Lóngzhì,
eating it will prevent you from becoming drowsy.
Another 120 *lǐ* to the west is
Mount Jiān,
the Jiān River originates there,
and flows north into the Yī River,
above there is much gold and jade,
below there is much blue realgar.
There is a tree there,
its appearance is like a crabapple but it has red leaves,
its name is Mángcǎo,
it can be used to poison fish.
Another 150 *lǐ* to the west is
Mount Dúsū,
which has no grass or trees but much water.
Another 200 *lǐ* to the west is
Mount Mànqú,
on which there is much gold and jade,
below there are many bamboo arrows.
The Yī River originates there,
and flows east into the Luò River.
There is a beast there,
its name is Mǎfù,
its appearance is like a human face and tiger's body,
its sound is like that of an infant,
and it eats people.
Altogether, the first of the Jì Mountain Range Scripture,
from Huīzhū Mountain to Mànqú Mountain,
totals nine mountains,
one thousand six hundred and seventy *lǐ*.
Their deities all have human faces and bird bodies.
Sacrifices use hair,
and one auspicious jade,
which is cast in without offering grain.
《Zhōng Cì Sān Jīng》, the first of Cí Mountain,
is called Ào'àn Mountain.
Its south side has an abundance of yíngfú jade,
and its north side has an abundance of ochre and
gold.
The deity Xūnchí dwells there.
It constantly produces fine jade.
To the north, one can see Hélín,
its appearance is like *qiàn* and like *jǔ*.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a white deer but with four antlers,
its name is Fūzhū,
When it appears, its town will suffer a great flood.
Ten *lǐ* further east,
is a mountain called Qīngyào zhī Shān,
truly it is the secret capital of the Di.
Looking north, one sees the bend of the Yellow River (Hé Qū);
many Jiàn-birds are there.
Looking south, one sees the Shàn-islet;
it is where the father of Yǔ (Yǔ fù) transformed.
Many *púléi* and
*púlú* are there.
The spirit Wǔ Luó governs it;
its appearance is a human face with leopard markings,
a small waist and white teeth,
and pierced ears with earrings.
Its cry is like the sound of jade.
This mountain
is suitable for women.
The Zhěn River originates here,
and flows north into the Yellow River.
There is a bird here,
named Yāo;
its appearance is like a wild duck (fú),
with a green body and red eyes and a red tail.
Eating it is beneficial for having children.
There is a grass here,
its appearance is like *jiān*,
with a square stem, yellow flowers, and red fruit.
Its root is like *gǎo běn* (藁本),
named *xún cǎo* (荀草),
taking it will give one the complexion of a beautiful woman.
Further east ten *lǐ*,
is called Guī Shān (騩山).
On it are beautiful jujubes,
and on its shady side is *yīng fú* (㻬琈) jade.
The Zhènghuí River (正回之水) originates here,
and flows north into the Yellow River.
In it are many flying fish,
their appearance is like pigs but with red markings.
Taking it will make one unafraid of thunder
and able to ward off weapons.
Further east forty *lǐ*,
is called Yí Sū zhī Shān (宜蘇之山).
On it are many metals and jades,
and below it are many *màn jū* (蔓居) trees.
The Yōngyōng River (滽滽之水) originates here,
and flows north into the Yellow River,
where there are many yellow cowries.
Further east twenty *lǐ*,
is called Hé Shān (和山).
On it there are no grasses or trees, but there is much *yáo bì* (瑤碧),
truly it is the nine capitals of the Yellow River.
This mountain has five bends,
The Jiǔshui River rises here,
converging and flowing north into the Yellow River.
Within it are many dark cyan jades.
The auspicious deity Tài Féng governs it.
Its appearance is like a human with a tiger tail.
It prefers to reside on the south-facing slope of Mount Cú,
and its comings and goings are accompanied by light.
The deity Tài Féng stirs the Qi of Heaven and Earth.
In general, the range of Mount Cú,
from Mount Áo'àn to Mount Hé,
comprises five mountains
spanning 440 *lǐ*.
To sacrifice to Tài Féng,
Xūnchí,
and Wǔluó, offer one male goat as the primary offering,
adorned with auspicious jade.
For the second two deities, bury one male chicken as an offering,
and use fine rice as the offering ingredient.
《Zhōng Cì Sì Jīng》The first of the Lí mountain range,
is called Mount Lùtí,
which has abundant jade on its summit
and abundant metal at its base.
The Gānshui River rises here,
flowing north into the Luò River,
within which are many *hán* stones.
Fifty *lǐ* to the west,
is called Mount Fúzhū,
on which there are many grindstones.
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a raccoon but with human eyes,
its name is *hú*.
The Guó River originates here,
and flows north into the Luò River,
in which there are many beautiful stones.
Again, one hundred and twenty *lǐ* to the west,
is called Mount Lí,
its south slope has much jade,
its north slope has much *sōu* (a kind of plant).
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like an ox,
with a blue-gray body,
its sound is like that of an infant,
it eats people,
its name is *xīqú*.
The Yōngyōng River originates here,
and flows south into the Yī River.
There is a beast there,
named *yú*,
its appearance is like a *nòuq犬* dog but with scales,
its fur is like boar bristles.
Again, two hundred *lǐ* to the west,
It is called Jī Wěi zhī Shān 箕尾之山,
it has abundant paper mulberry trees,
and abundant túshí 涂石 rocks.
On its summit, there are abundant yīngfú zhī yù 㻬琈之玉 jade.
Two hundred and fifty *lǐ* further west,
it is called Bǐng Shān 柄山,
on its summit there is abundant jade,
and at its base there is abundant copper.
The Tāodiāo zhī Shuǐ 滔雕之水 River originates here,
and flows north into the Luò 洛 River.
In it there are abundant yán yáng 羬羊 wild sheep.
There is a tree,
its appearance is like the ailanthus tree,
its leaves are like the paulownia and it has pods for fruit,
its name is bà 茇,
which can be used to poison fish.
Two hundred *lǐ* further west,
it is called Bái Biān zhī Shān 白邊之山,
on its summit there is abundant gold and jade,
and at its base there is abundant green realgar.
Two hundred *lǐ* further west,
it is called Xióng'ěr zhī Shān 熊耳之山,
on its summit there is abundant lacquer,
and at its base there are abundant palm trees.
The Fúháo zhī Shuǐ 浮濠之水 River originates here,
It flows westward and empties into the Luò River;
within it are many water jades,
and many "people-fish" (rén yú).
There is a grass,
its appearance is like sū but with red flowers,
named tíng lì;
it can be used to poison fish.
300 li further west is called Mǔ Mountain.
On its top, there is much patterned stone;
at its base, there is much bamboo for arrows, and
bamboo for baskets.
Among the animals, there are many tuó cattle and
quán sheep.
Among the birds, there are many red bì pheasants.
350 li further west is called Huānjǔ Mountain.
The Luò River originates there and
flows northeast, emptying into the Xuánhù River.
Within it are many things like horse intestines.
These two mountains
are located between the Luò River.
In total, the head of the Lí Mountain range,
from Lùtí Mountain to Xuánhù Mountain,
includes nine mountains in total,
One thousand six hundred and seventy *lǐ*.
The appearance of their spirits is all human-faced and beast-bodied.
To sacrifice to them,
a single white chicken is used as an offering,
praying but not using *xǔ* (grain offering),
and adorning them with colorful clothing.
*Zhōng Cì Wǔ Jīng*: The head of Bóshān Mountain,
called Gǒuchuáng Mountain,
has no grass or trees,
and is full of strange rocks.
Three hundred *lǐ* to the east,
is Shǒu Mountain.
Its northern (shady) side has much *gǔ zuò*,
and the grass is mostly *xiān yuán*.
Its southern (sunny) side has much *hán fú* jade,
and the trees are mostly pagoda trees (*huái*);
on its northern side there is a valley,
called Jīgǔ Valley,
which has many *xiū* birds.
Their appearance is like an owl but with three eyes,
and ears.
Their sound is like *lù*.
Eating it can cure *diàn* (prolapse of the anus).
Three hundred *lǐ* further east,
is Xuánzhú Mountain.
No grass or trees,
but many patterned stones.
Three hundred *lǐ* further east is
called Mount Cōnglóng,
where there are no grass or trees,
but many *zhào* stones.
Five hundred *lǐ* northeast is
called Mount Tiáogǔ,
where the trees are mostly locust and *tóng* trees,
and the grass is mostly peony and *xiū*
*dōng*.
Ten *lǐ* further north is
called Mount Chāo,
where the north-facing slopes have much azure jade,
and the south-facing slopes have a well,
with water in winter but drying up in summer.
Five hundred *lǐ* further east is
called Mount Chénghóu,
where there are many *chūn* trees on top,
and much *qiú* grass.
Five hundred *lǐ* further east is
called Mount Zhāogē,
where the valleys have much beautiful white clay.
Another five hundred *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Huái (Huái Shān).
Its valleys contain much gold and tin.
Another ten *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Lì (Lì Shān).
Its trees are mostly locust trees,
and its southern slope contains much jade.
Another ten *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Shī (Shī Shān).
It has much cyan jade,
and its animals are mostly *jīng* deer.
The Shī River (Shī Shuǐ) originates here,
flowing south to empty into the Luò River (Luò Shuǐ),
which contains much fine jade.
Another ten *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Liángyú (Liángyú zhī Shān).
Its summit has much *gǔ* and *zuò* trees,
and no rocks.
The Yú River (Yú Shuǐ) originates on its northern slope,
flowing north to empty into the Yellow River (Hé);
the Rǔ River (Rǔ Shuǐ) originates on its southern slope,
flowing southeast to empty into the Luò River (Luò).
Another ten *lǐ* to the southeast is called Mount Gǔwěi (Gǔwěi zhī Shān).
It is called Gǔwěi Mountain,
with many whetstones and
red copper.
The Lóngyú River originates here,
flowing southeast and emptying into the Luò River.
Twenty *lǐ* northeast again,
it is called Shēng Mountain,
its trees are mostly paper mulberry, oak, and jujube,
its plants are mostly *shūyú* and fragrant orchid,
with many *kòutuō* plants.
The Huángsuān River originates here,
flowing north and emptying into the Yellow River,
in which there are many *xuányù* jades.
Twelve *lǐ* east again,
it is called Yángxū Mountain,
with much gold,
overlooking the Xuánhù River.
In total, the mountain range headed by Bó Mountain,
from Gǒulín Mountain to Yángxū Mountain,
comprises sixteen mountains in all,
spanning two thousand nine hundred and eighty-two *lǐ*.
Shēng Mountain
is a burial ground.
Its sacrificial rites:
a complete ox, sheep and pig,
Yīng uses auspicious jade.
Shǒu Shān,
is a spirit.
Its sacrifice uses glutinous rice,
black sacrificial animals,
the complete offerings of a great sacrifice,
and sprouted-grain liquor.
They perform the shield dance
and set up drums.
Yīng uses one bì jade disc.
Shī River,
unites with Heaven.
They sacrifice to it with a fat animal,
using one black dog on the upper bank,
and one female chicken on the lower bank.
They cut open one female sheep
and offer its blood.
Yīng uses auspicious jade,
decorates it with colors,
and offers it in a feast.
"The Sixth Classic of the Central Series": The beginning of Gǎo Dī Mountain
is called Píngféng Mountain.
From the south, it overlooks the Yī and Luò rivers;
from the east, it overlooks Gǔchéng Mountain.
There is no grass or trees,
and the water contains much sand and stone.
There is a spirit there,
Its form is like a human but with two heads.
Its name is Jiāo Chóng (驕蟲).
It is a stinging insect.
In reality, it is the dwelling place of honey.
To offer sacrifices to it:
Use one male rooster.
Pray for good fortune and do not kill it.
Ten *lǐ* to the west,
is called Gǎo Dī zhī Shān (縞羝之山).
There are no grasses or trees.
There is much gold and jade.
Again, ten *lǐ* to the west,
is called Wěi Shān (廆山).
On its northern side there is much fine jade.
To its west there is a valley,
named Guàn Gǔ (雚谷).
Its trees are mostly willows and paper mulberry trees.
Within it there is a bird,
its form is like a pheasant but with a long tail,
as red as crimson fire and with a blue beak,
its name is Líng Yú (鴒䳩), its cry is its own name,
if consumed, one will not suffer from impaired vision.
The Jiāo Shāng zhī (交觴之) River
springs from its southern side,
and flows south, emptying into the Luò (洛) River;
The Yú Suí zhī (俞隨之) River springs from its northern side,
and flows north into the Gǔ River.
Thirty *lǐ* further west,
is called Zhānzhū zhī Shān (瞻諸之山),
whose southern side has abundant gold,
and whose northern side has abundant variegated stones. The Xiè River (㴬水) originates here,
and flows southeast into the Luò River.
The Shǎo River (少水) originates on its northern side,
and flows east into the Gǔ River.
Thirty *lǐ* further west,
is called Lóuzhuō zhī Shān (婁涿之山),
which has no vegetation,
but abundant gold and jade.
The Zhān River (瞻水) originates on its southern side,
and flows east into the Luò River.
The Bēi River (陂水) originates on its northern side,
and flows north into the Gǔ River,
within which there are abundant *zǐshí* (茈石) and
variegated stones.
Forty *lǐ* further west,
is called Báishí zhī Shān (白石之山).
The Huì River (惠水) originates on its southern side,
and flows south into the Luò River,
within which there are abundant water jade.
The Jiàn River (澗水) originates on its northern side,
and flows northwest into the Gǔ River,
Among them are many míshí (麋石) and
lúdān (櫨丹).
Fifty *lǐ* further west is
Gǔ Shān (穀山).
On its summit grows abundant *gǔ* (穀),
and below it grows abundant mulberry.
The Shuǎng River (爽水) rises here,
and flows northwest, emptying into the Gǔ River (穀水).
Within it are many bìlǜ (碧綠).
Seventy-two *lǐ* further west is
Mì Shān (密山).
On its sunny side is abundant jade,
and on its shady side is abundant iron.
The Háo River (豪水) rises here,
and flows south, emptying into the Luò River (洛).
Within it are many xuánguī (旋龜),
which have the appearance of a bird's head and a turtle's tail,
and whose sound is like splitting wood.

its trees are mostly *chū* (樗) ailanthus and willow,
its grasses are mostly *kòu tuō* (寇脫) *Astragalus complanatus*.
Again, 140 *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Guī (騩山),
its sunny side has much beautiful jade and red gold,
its shady side has much iron,
its trees are mostly peach branches, *jīng qǐ* (荊芑).
Again, 200 *lǐ* to the east is called Mount Gé (葛山),
above it is much red gold,
below it is much *jiān shí* (瑊石) hard stone,
its trees are mostly *zū* (柤) wild dates, chestnut, mandarin orange, *yòu* (櫾) citrus, *yóu* (楢) oak, and *niǔ* (杻) shrub.
The animals there are mostly líng dì.
The plants there are mostly jiā róng.
Another 170 *lǐ* to the east is
called Mount Jiǎchāo,
whose sunny side has much yellow white clay,
and whose shady side has much fine red clay.
The trees there are mostly zā lì jú yòu,
and within it are many lóng xiū.
In all, the head of the Mín Mountains,
from Mount Nǚjǐ to Mount Jiǎchāo,
includes sixteen mountains,
covering three thousand five hundred *lǐ*.
The forms of their deities are all with the body of a horse and the head of a dragon.
Their sacrifices:
Bury a male chicken for the hair,
and use cooked glutinous rice for the offerings.
Mount Wén,
Gōunǐ,
Fēngyǔ,
and Mount Guī,
these are all large mounds.
Their sacrifices:
Offer wine,
provide the shǎoláo offerings,
and bury one auspicious jade with hair.
Mount Xióng,
To Dì (帝)
, its sacrificial rites:
Offerings of wine,
complete Grand Sacrificial Offering (dà láo jù 大牢具),
and a jade disc (bì 璧) with infant animal hair.
Use shields in dance,
to avert misfortune through military performance;
For praying, wear jade pendant ornaments (qiú 璆) and ceremonial headdress (miǎn 冕) for dance.
The first of the *Zhong Ci Shi Jing* (中次十經)
is called Shǒu Yáng zhī Shān (首陽之山),
on it are abundant gold and jade,
but no grass or trees.
Fifty *lǐ* (里) further west,
is called Hǔ Wěi zhī Shān (虎尾之山),
its trees are mostly prickly ash and *jū* trees,
and many large sealed stones,
its southern side has much copper ore,
and its northern side has much iron.
Fifty *lǐ* (里) further southwest,
is called Fán Huì zhī Shān (繁繢之山),
its trees are mostly *yóu* and *niǔ* trees,
its grasses are mostly *zhīgōu* grass.
Twenty *lǐ* (里) further southwest,
is called Yǒng Shí zhī Shān (勇石之山),
No grass or trees;
Abundant white metal;
Abundant water.
Twenty *lǐ* further west,
is a mountain called Fù Zhōu zhī Shān;
its trees are mostly sandalwood;
on its southern slope is abundant gold.
There is a bird,
its appearance is like an owl,
but it has one foot and a pig's tail;
its name is Qǐ Zhǒng;
if it appears, then there will be a great plague in that country.
Thirty *lǐ* further west,
is a mountain called Chǔ Shān;
abundant parasitic trees;
abundant pepper trees and *jū*;
abundant *zhè*;
abundant white clay.
Twenty *lǐ* further west,
is a mountain called Yòu Yuán zhī Shān;
on its southern slope is abundant blue *qīng chè*;
on its northern slope is abundant iron;
its birds are mostly mynas.
Fifty *lǐ* further west,
It is called Zhuō Shān 涿山.
Its trees are mostly găo 榖, zuò 柞, and niǔ 杻.
On its sunny side, there is much jǐng fú 㻬琈 jade.
Seventy *lǐ* further west,
it is called Bǐng Shān 丙山.
Its trees are mostly zǐ 梓 and tán 檀.
There are many shěn niǔ 弞杻.
In all, the beginning of the Shǒu Yáng Shān 首陽山 range,
from Shǒu Shān 首山 to Bǐng Shān 丙山,
is nine mountains in all,
totaling two hundred and sixty-seven *lǐ*.
The appearance of their deities is all dragon bodies with human faces.
To sacrifice to them:
bury the hair of one rooster,
and use five types of offerings.
Dǔ Shān 堵山
is a tomb;
to sacrifice to it:
prepare a *shǎo láo* 少牢,
offer wine,
and bury the downy hair of a jade disk.
Guī Shān 騩山
is an emperor;
when sacrificing to it, offer wine,
prepare a *tài láo* 太牢;
have two shamans dance together,
Yīng offered a bi jade.
*Zhōng Cì Yī Shí Yī Shān Jīng* (The Classic of the Central Range, Section One, Mountain Eleven): The head of the Jīng Mountain,
is called Yìwàng Mountain.
The Tuān River originates here,
flowing east to empty into the Jì River.
The Kuàng River originates here,
flowing southeast to empty into the Hàn River,
and it contains many jiāo (dragons/crocodiles).
Its top has many pines and cypresses,
and its base has much lacquer and catalpa trees,
its sunny side has much red gold,
and its shady side has much mín (a kind of stone).
Another one hundred and fifty *lǐ* to the northeast,
is called Zhāogē Mountain.
The Wǔ River originates here,
flowing southeast to empty into the Róng River,
and it contains many merpeople.
Its top has much catalpa and Phoebe zhennan trees,
and its animals are mostly língmí (antelope-like creatures).
There is a plant there,
named Mǎng Grass,
which can be used to poison fish.
Another two hundred *lǐ* to the southeast,
is called Dìqūn Mountain,
its sunny side has much beautiful yáo fú jade,
Its shady side has much iron.
The Dì Qūn (帝囷) River issues forth from its top,
and flows hidden beneath it.
It has many Míng Shé (鳴蛇) (calling snakes).
Another fifty *lǐ* to the southeast is
Shì Shān (視山).
Its top has much chives.
There is a well there,
named Tiān Jǐng (天井) (Heavenly Well).
In summer it has water,
in winter it is dry.
Its top has much mulberry,
much beautiful white clay,
gold, and jade.
Another two hundred *lǐ* to the southeast is
Qián Shān (前山) (Front Mountain).
Its trees are mostly *zhū* (櫧) (oak),
and much cypress.
Its sunny side has much gold,
its shady side has much ochre.
Another three hundred *lǐ* to the southeast is
Fēng Shān (豐山).
There is a beast there,
its appearance is like a monkey,
with red eyes,
It has a red beak and
a yellow body.
It is named Yōnghé.
Its appearance foretells great fear in the country.
The spirit Gēng Fǔ resides there.
It often roams the clear and cold depths.
Its appearances and disappearances are accompanied by light.
Its appearance foretells the ruin of that country.
There are nine bells there
that know when frost will sound.
Much gold is found on its top,
and below there are many *gǔ* 榖, *zuò* 柞, *niǔ* 杻, and *jiāng* 橿 trees.
Further northeast for eight hundred *lǐ*,
is called Mount Tùchuáng.
Its southern side has much iron.
Its trees have much *shūyú*.
Its grasses have much *jīgǔ*.
Its root is like a chicken egg.
Its taste is sour and sweet.
Those who eat it are beneficial to people.
Further east for sixty *lǐ*,
is called Mount Pí.
There is much white clay
and much red ochre.
Its trees have much pine and cypress.
Sixty *lǐ* further east is
Yáobì Mountain.
Its trees are mostly catalpa and *nán* trees.
On its shady side, there is much blue *qīngchú*;
on its sunny side, there is much white gold.
There is a bird there
which looks like a pheasant,
and constantly eats *fēi*.
It is called a *zhèn*.
Forty *lǐ* further east is
Gōnglí Mountain.
The Yù River rises here
and flows south into the Hàn River.
There is a bird there
called Yīngsháo,
which looks like a magpie,
with red eyes,
a red beak,
and a white body.
Its tail is shaped like a spoon,
and its call is like its own name.
There are many *mó* cattle
and many *xiányáng* sheep.
Fifty *lǐ* further northeast is
Zhìhù Mountain,
which is covered with pine, cypress, *jī* and *huán* trees.
One hundred *lǐ* further northwest is
Jǐnlǐ Mountain,
which is covered with pine and cypress trees
and many beautiful catalpa trees.
On its shady side, there is much red *dānchú*.
They first headed south.
The Dōnmù Guó (Deep-Eyed Country) is to its east.
Its people each hold one hand and have one eye.
It is east of the Gònggōng Terrace.
The Wúcháng zhī Guó (Country Without Intestines) is east of the Dōnmù.
Its people are tall and have no intestines.
The Niè'ěr zhī Guó (Country of Pinched Ears) is east of the Wúcháng Guó.
They employ two striped tigers.
Its people use both hands to pinch their ears.
They live suspended in the sea.
And from the waters come forth strange objects.
The two tigers are to their east.
Kuāfù raced after the sun.
He entered the sun.
Thirsty, he wanted to drink.
He drank from the Yellow River and the Wei River.
The Yellow River and the Wei River were not enough.
He headed north to drink from the great marsh.
He had not arrived
when he died of thirst on the way.
He abandoned his staff,
which transformed into the Dènglín forest.
The Bófù Guó (Country of Broad Shoulders) is east of the Niè'ěr.
Its people are large.
With their right hand they hold a blue snake,
and with their left hand they hold a yellow snake.
The Dènglín forest is to their east,
consisting of two trees.
One is called Bófù.
